## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{20}{20}{20}{20}{100}}

_Why does passing dozens of consecutive real-world hardware trials provide almost zero mathematical assurance that an embodied autonomous system is safe?_

In standard machine learning systems, evaluation relies on static held-out validation or test splits: one computes Top-1 classification accuracy, token perplexity, or F1 score over $10^4$ or $10^5$ independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) test samples. If an offline model achieves 99.9 percent Top-1 accuracy or negligible validation loss on frozen test splits, the system is conventionally declared production-ready. In software ML engineering, that evaluation is passive, memoryless, and computationally cheap: misclassifying validation sample $k$ does not alter sample $k+1$ ($\partial x_{k+1} / \partial \hat{y}_k = 0$), and rerunning an entire evaluation suite consumes merely a few GPU minutes with zero hardware degradation. Flash that identical neural policy onto physical hardware, however, and the robot can crash into a fixture or wedge a mechanical latch within seconds. In Physical AI, actions cross the causal boundary into mass, momentum, and non-smooth contact mechanics. The policy's admitted actions physically move the plant, endogenously generating subsequent sensory observations ($s_{t+1} = f(s_t, u_t)$). Minor prediction errors that appear trivial under open-loop regression metrics compound quadratically ($\mathcal{O}(T^2 \epsilon)$) into catastrophic boundary excursions.

Furthermore, evaluating physical systems exposes an irreconcilable collision between statistical sample-size scaling and hardware endurance. In academic ML, scoring twenty consecutive successes across twenty test samples yields an empirical success rate of $\hat{p} = 1.00$. When standard ML practitioners construct familiar Central Limit Theorem Wald confidence intervals ($p \pm z \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n}$), the estimated sample variance vanishes identically at zero failures ($k=n$), collapsing the interval to $[1.0, 1.0]$—a mathematically absurd claim of certain reliability from merely twenty runs. Exact non-asymptotic binomial inversion reveals the sobering reality: twenty clean runs bound true operational reliability at only 86.1 percent at 95 percent confidence, leaving a staggering 13.9 percent upper failure probability. Certifying high-assurance Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) metrics through brute-force physical trials demands tens of thousands of failure-free operating hours—surpassing mechanical bearing fatigue life ($L_{10}$) and cycling motor windings past their thermal breakdown limits.

Concluding Part II (Policy Synthesis), this chapter replaces static benchmark scores with closed-loop statistical sequential testing. We develop exact Clopper-Pearson binomial lower bounds, the Poisson Rule of Three ($T \ge 3.0/\lambda$), and Abraham Wald's Sequential Probability Ratio Test (SPRT) likelihood-ratio martingales bounded by Ville's maximal inequality. We analyze the steep 24-fold evidentiary penalty of physical failures, formulate the Average Sample Number (ASN) scaling with Kullback-Leibler divergence, map the four evaluation evidence regimes, derive the sim-to-real proxy transfer law, and construct the cryptographic evaluation record that governs the formal handoff to Part III's deterministic runtime enforcement.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Interpret physical success rates as conditional evidence about a specified machine, environment, and trial protocol
- Compare open-loop prediction accuracy with closed-loop behavior shaped by the policy's own actions
- Select the evidence regime (replay, simulation, shadow operation, or constrained physical testing) that can answer a given evaluation question
- Calculate trial counts and test time needed to support a stated reliability target
- Derive exact non-asymptotic Clopper-Pearson lower bounds and the Poisson Rule of Three when evaluating zero-failure physical campaigns
- Formulate Abraham Wald's Sequential Probability Ratio Test (SPRT) using likelihood-ratio martingales and Ville's maximal inequality to bound Type I error under continuous inspection
- Analyze the 24-fold evidentiary penalty of physical failures and Average Sample Number (ASN) scaling with Kullback-Leibler divergence
- Formulate intervention-based physical metrics—Autonomous Completion Rate (ACR), Mean Time Between Interventions (MTBI), Intervention Density ($D_{\text{int}}$), and Reset Latency ($T_{\text{reset}}$)—to replace scalar pass rates and prevent the censored trial fallacy
- Quantify how hardware instance variance (gear backlash, link compliance, sensor mounting tolerances) and environmental unobservables break sample stationarity across robot units
- Evaluate which rare failures remain unsupported by feasible testing and the available statistical assumptions
- Design a predeclared trial protocol with fixed outcome rules and full-denominator accounting of interventions and aborts
- Construct an evaluation record that confines its claim to a target operating domain and assigns uncovered conditions to runtime monitors

:::

## Empirical Bounds of Small-Sample Survival Verification {#sec-evaluation-closed-loop-survival}

```{python}
#| label: calc-evaluation-door-campaign
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE DOOR CAMPAIGN ON THE RUNNING MACHINE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: chapter opener, @sec-evaluation-logs, and the lease fallacy.
# │ Show: the evaluated campaign (latch task, base stopped) and the machine
# │       values the chapter quotes: approach speed, tripwire, latch limit, rack
# │       capacity, chunk period, and chunk lease; plus the Part II funnel
# │       the completed record carries (ledger cells, supported cells,
# │       known absences, manifest omissions).
# │ How: registry fields of the warehouse mobile manipulator and its aisle;
# │      the standoff and the ledger counts (from @sec-data and
# │      @sec-training) are chapter-local inputs.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_latency, fmt_force, fmt_mass, fmt_frequency, check, MarkdownStr

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EvalMachine:
    """The latch campaign Ch7 evaluates, on the book's running machine."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    standoff = 2.0 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative; base start distance from the door
    v_approach = AISLE.v_latch_approach  # category: illustrative; guarded approach, the declared ODD's speed
    f_latch_limit = AISLE.f_latch_limit  # category: illustrative; latch damage limit
    f_trip = AISLE.f_latch_tripwire  # category: illustrative; contact tripwire that ends an attempt (@sec-data)
    rack_capacity = RM.onboard_payload_capacity  # category: chosen; tote-rack capacity
    chunk_rate = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen; chunk policy rate
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen; chunk lease
    n_plate_positions = 3  # category: illustrative; nominal and two displaced plates, the scenario ledger of @sec-data
    ledger_speeds = [AISLE.v_latch_approach, AISLE.v_latch_high]  # category: illustrative; the ledger's two approach speeds
    n_supported = 1  # category: illustrative; the nominal plate at the guarded approach (LatchScenarioLedger in @sec-data)
    n_omissions = 2  # category: illustrative; soft penalty contact and missing transport lag, the manifest's omission log

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    chunk_period = (1 / chunk_rate).to(millisecond)
    n_speeds = len(ledger_speeds)
    n_cells = n_plate_positions * n_speeds
    n_absences = n_cells - n_supported

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v_approach.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second).magnitude - 0.03) < 1e-9, "Guarded approach is not 0.03 m/s")
    check(abs(f_latch_limit.to(newton).magnitude - 100.0) < 1e-9, "Latch limit is not 100 N")
    check(abs(f_trip.to(newton).magnitude - 15.0) < 1e-9, "Contact tripwire is not 15 N")
    check(f_trip < f_latch_limit, "The tripwire must end an attempt well below the damage limit")
    check(abs(rack_capacity.to(kilogram).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Tote-rack capacity is not 50 kg")
    check(abs(chunk_period.to(millisecond).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Chunk period is not 50 ms")
    check(abs(t_lease.to(millisecond).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, "Chunk lease is not 60 ms")
    check(chunk_period < t_lease, "Chunk period must fit inside the lease")
    check(n_cells == 6 and n_supported == 1 and n_absences == 5, "Ledger should have one supported cell of six (matches @sec-data)")
    check(n_omissions == 2, "Manifest omission log holds two unclosed departures (matches @sec-training)")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    standoff_str = fmt_length(standoff, precision=0)
    v_approach_str = fmt_velocity(v_approach, precision=2)
    f_latch_limit_str = fmt_force(f_latch_limit, precision=0)
    f_trip_str = fmt_force(f_trip, precision=0)
    rack_capacity_str = fmt_mass(rack_capacity, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    chunk_rate_str = fmt_frequency(chunk_rate)
    chunk_period_str = fmt_latency(chunk_period)
    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(t_lease)
    _words = {1: "one", 2: "two", 3: "three", 5: "five", 6: "six"}
    n_plate_positions_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_plate_positions])
    n_speeds_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_speeds])
    n_cells_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_cells])
    n_supported_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_supported])
    n_absences_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_absences])
    n_omissions_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_omissions])
```

Fresh from the offline training pipeline, `latch-bc-01` is flashed onto the warehouse mobile manipulator; it is the one checkpoint the policy manifest of @sec-training-policy-manifest declares evaluable. In initial validation, the machine completes twenty consecutive runs of its door task. Each run starts with the base `{python} EvalMachine.standoff_str` (illustrative; see the Reader Guide) from the spring-latched cage door; the base drives in and stops, and with the base at rest the arm unlatches and opens the door at the `{python} EvalMachine.v_approach_str` guarded approach, without a contact-tripwire crossing or a human intervention. Its empirical sample success rate is $\hat{p} = 1.00$ (100 percent). In static machine learning benchmarks, scoring $\hat{p} = 1.00$ across an evaluation batch is often celebrated as an empirical triumph. In physical AI systems engineering, that record leaves the deployment decision unresolved, because twenty clean runs establish only a bounded statistical lower limit and leave substantial uncertainty about unobserved failures.

```{python}
#| label: calc-evaluation-clopper-pearson-zero-failure
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CLOPPER-PEARSON ZERO-FAILURE RELIABILITY SIZING (LEGO)

# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-evaluation-derivation-20-run-lower-bound, @sec-evaluation-logs, and the takeaways.
# │ Show: One-sided confidence limits for iid zero-failure trials, not a rate estimate.
# │ How: p_lower = alpha^(1/n); failure_upper = 1 - p_lower.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_percent, fmt_int, fmt, check, MarkdownStr

class ClopperPearsonZeroFailure:
    """Exact binomial confidence bounds for physical robotics qualification."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    n_runs = 20  # category: illustrative; the opening campaign's clean runs
    confidence = 0.95  # category: chosen; one-sided confidence level
    alpha = 1.0 - confidence  # category: derived; significance level
    n_one_in = 8  # category: illustrative; a policy that fails one run in eight
    n_fallacy = 1000  # category: illustrative; clean openings in the perfect-record fallacy
    n_looks = 5  # category: illustrative; independent 5 percent looks in the optional-stopping example

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    p_lower = calc_clopper_pearson_zero_failure_bound(n_runs, confidence=confidence)
    failure_upper = 1.0 - p_lower
    p_clean_one_in = (1.0 - 1.0 / n_one_in) ** n_runs  # chance that policy still logs n_runs clean runs

    # Scaling to 99.9% reliability
    p_target_999 = 0.999
    n_req_999 = calc_zero_failure_sample_size(p_target_999, confidence=confidence)
    p_lower_fallacy = calc_clopper_pearson_zero_failure_bound(n_fallacy, confidence=confidence)
    p_any_false_positive = 1.0 - (1.0 - alpha) ** n_looks  # chance of at least one false positive across independent looks

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(p_lower - 0.8609) < 0.001, "Unexpected 20-run lower bound")
    check(abs(failure_upper - 0.1391) < 0.001, "Unexpected 20-run upper confidence limit")
    check(n_req_999 == 2995, "Unexpected sample size for 99.9% reliability")
    check(n_one_in == 8 and abs(p_clean_one_in - 0.0692) < 0.001, "Unexpected clean-record probability for a one-in-eight policy")
    check(p_lower_fallacy < p_target_999 and abs(p_lower_fallacy - 0.9970) < 0.0001, "The 1,000-run bound must fall short of 99.9 percent")
    check(abs(p_any_false_positive - 0.2262) < 0.001, "Five independent 5 percent looks should give about 22.6 percent")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    n_runs_str = fmt_int(n_runs)
    confidence_pct_str = fmt_percent(confidence, precision=0)
    p_lower_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_lower, precision=1)
    failure_upper_pct_str = fmt_percent(failure_upper, precision=1)
    p_lower_val_str = fmt(p_lower, precision=3)
    n_req_999_str = fmt_int(n_req_999, commas=True)
    _words = {5: "five", 8: "eight"}
    n_one_in_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_one_in])
    p_clean_one_in_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_clean_one_in, precision=1)
    n_fallacy_str = fmt_int(n_fallacy, commas=True)
    p_lower_fallacy_str = fmt(p_lower_fallacy, precision=4)
    n_looks_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_looks].capitalize())
    p_any_false_positive_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_any_false_positive, precision=1)
```

The familiar Wald confidence interval ($p \pm z_{1-\alpha/2} \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n}$) that standard ML practitioners rely on for classification error bars cannot describe that physical uncertainty. Derived from Central Limit Theorem asymptotic normality approximations, the Wald interval assumes the sampling distribution of the sample mean $\hat{p} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n Y_i$ converges to a Gaussian $\mathcal{N}(p, p(1-p)/n)$. In classical statistics, this normal approximation requires the textbook rule of thumb $n p \ge 10$ and $n (1-p) \ge 10$. When an evaluation yields zero failures ($k = n$ or $\hat{p} = 1.0$), the failure count is $n(1-\hat{p}) = 0$, violating the CLT condition completely. At $k = n$, the estimated sample variance $\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n$ vanishes identically to zero ($1.0 \times 0.0 / n = 0$). The estimated standard error collapses to zero, and the Wald interval degenerates to the single point $[1.0, 1.0]$—a mathematically absurd claim of zero variance and absolute certainty from merely twenty runs. Even when failures do occur near the parameter boundaries ($p \approx 0$ or $p \approx 1$), symmetric Wald intervals routinely violate physical reality by producing lower bounds below zero or upper bounds above unity, and suffer from severe non-monotonic coverage oscillations where actual coverage drops to 60 or 70 percent despite a nominal 95 percent specification (as characterized by Brown, Cai, and DasGupta).

Furthermore, in safety-critical cyber-physical systems, symmetric two-sided intervals around an empirical mean are irrelevant; qualification requires establishing a rigorous **one-sided lower bound** on success probability ($p_{\text{lower}}$) or an upper bound on failure probability ($p_{\text{fail}} \le 1 - p_{\text{lower}}$), bounding minimum acceptable reliability at a declared significance level $\alpha$. The exact bound inverts the binomial cumulative distribution directly, eliminating all asymptotic approximations. For $k$ successes in $n$ independent Bernoulli trials, the exact one-sided Clopper-Pearson lower bound\index{Clopper-Pearson non-asymptotic bound!definition}\index{Clopper-Pearson method} [@clopper1934use] at significance level $\alpha$ is the value $p_{\text{lower}}$ satisfying:
$$P(K \ge k \mid p = p_{\text{lower}}) = \sum_{j=k}^n \binom{n}{j} p_{\text{lower}}^j (1 - p_{\text{lower}})^{n-j} = \alpha$$
Formally, this exact tail inversion corresponds to the lower $\alpha$-quantile of the Beta distribution: $p_{\text{lower}} = I^{-1}_\alpha(k, n - k + 1) = \text{Beta}(\alpha; k, n - k + 1)$. When an evaluation logs zero failures ($k = n$), this binomial sum collapses to a single monomial: the joint probability of $n$ consecutive independent successes by chance is simply $p^n$. Equating this to the false-optimism significance level $\alpha = 0.05$ directly yields the exact closed-form lower bound:
$$p_{\text{lower}} = \alpha^{1/n}$$
and the corresponding exact upper bound on failure probability:
$$p_{\text{fail, upper}} = 1 - \alpha^{1/n}$$
For rare failure rates ($p_{\text{fail}} \ll 1$), we obtain the celebrated **Rule of Three**\index{Rule of Three} [@hanley1983nothing] via first-order Taylor expansion: $\ln(1 - p_{\text{fail}}) = -p_{\text{fail}} - \frac{p_{\text{fail}}^2}{2} - \dots \approx -p_{\text{fail}}$. Setting the zero-failure probability $(1 - p_{\text{fail}})^n = \alpha = 0.05$ implies $n \ln(1 - p_{\text{fail}}) = \ln(0.05) \approx -2.9957 \approx -3.0$. Substituting the linear expansion yields $-n p_{\text{fail}} \approx -3.0$, establishing that when $n$ independent trials pass with zero failures, the upper 95 percent confidence bound on failure probability is approximately:
$$p_{\text{fail, upper}}^{95\%} \approx \frac{3}{n}.$$ {#eq-eval-rule-of-three}
For the twenty door runs, @eq-eval-rule-of-three yields $p_{\text{fail, upper}}^{95\%} \approx 3/20 = 0.15$. The exact computation in \ref{nbk-evaluation-derivation-20-run-lower-bound} tightens this to a `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.failure_upper_pct_str` percent failure upper limit, which leaves the machine far short of 95 percent demonstrated reliability. Crucially, this non-asymptotic formulation demonstrates why **twenty trials cannot prove 99 percent reliability**. To mathematically certify a 99 percent operational reliability lower bound ($p_{\text{target}} = 0.99$, or $p_{\text{fail}} = 0.01$) at 95 percent confidence ($\alpha = 0.05$), the required zero-failure sample size inverts to:
$$n = \left\lceil \frac{\ln(\alpha)}{\ln(p_{\text{target}})} \right\rceil = \left\lceil \frac{\ln(0.05)}{\ln(0.99)} \right\rceil = \left\lceil \frac{-2.99573}{-0.01005} \right\rceil = 299 \text{ consecutive trials}$$
By contrast, twenty consecutive failure-free runs certify a lower bound of merely $p_{\text{lower}} = (0.05)^{1/20} \approx 0.8609$ (86.1 percent), leaving a massive 13.9 percent probability of physical failure unrefuted. Believing that twenty clean runs demonstrate a 99 percent reliable machine is an error of almost fifteen-fold in statistical exposure ($299$ versus $20$). A defective policy that fails once in every `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_one_in_str` runs ($p = 0.875$) still completes twenty consecutive runs cleanly `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_clean_one_in_pct_str` percent of the time—meaning that more than one out of every fifteen qualification campaigns will certify a dangerously flawed checkpoint purely by chance.[^fn-math-rule-three]

Moreover, this statistical bound assumes stationary, identically distributed draws across trials—an assumption routinely shattered on physical testbeds by **hardware instance variance**. If twenty trials are executed on a single physical robot (Unit 01), they characterize that unit's individual harmonic drive gear backlash ($\Delta \theta_{\text{backlash}} \sim 1\text{ mrad}$), motor torque constant tolerance ($\pm 5$ percent), and sensor mounting alignment. When deployed onto Unit 02, differing machining tolerances, gear backlash, and structural compliance alter the physical transfer function, converting nominal runs into latch jams without changing a single neural weight.

[^fn-math-rule-three]: **Continuous-time Poisson equivalence of the Rule of Three**: The Rule of Three applies equally to continuous-time Poisson processes with constant hazard rate $\lambda$. If an autonomous machine operates for total failure-free duration $T$ without an intervention, the probability of zero Poisson arrivals is $P(N(T) = 0) = e^{-\lambda T}$. Equating this to significance level $\alpha = 0.05$ yields $-\lambda T = \ln(0.05) \approx -2.9957$, proving that the 95 percent upper confidence limit on failure rate is $\lambda_{\text{upper}} \approx 3.0/T$, or conversely that bounding $\lambda \le \lambda_{\text{target}}$ requires exposure time $T \ge 3.0 / \lambda_{\text{target}}$. To certify a target Mean Time Between Failures of $\text{MTBF} = 1/\lambda_{\text{target}}$, an autonomous system must execute uninterrupted physical testing for at least three times the target MTBF ($T \ge 3.0 \times \text{MTBF}$) without a single failure or intervention.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_nonasymptotic_reliability_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Vertical ladder comparing trial sample sizes against achievable statistical reliability bounds."}
*Twenty consecutive zero-failure runs bound reliability at only 86 percent, requiring thousands of runs for high-assurance certification.*
:::

::: {#nbk-evaluation-derivation-20-run-lower-bound .callout-notebook title="Derivation of the 20-run lower bound"}
**Problem**: The mobile manipulator completes $n =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_runs_str` physical door-opening runs with zero contact-tripwire crossings or human interventions ($k =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_runs_str`). What is the exact one-sided `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.confidence_pct_str` percent lower confidence bound on its true operational success probability $p$?

**Mathematical Derivation**: For independent, identically distributed Bernoulli trials from the declared operational test distribution, $p_{\text{lower}}$ is the success probability at which `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_runs_str` consecutive successes have probability $\alpha=0.05$. Thus the one-sided 95 percent lower confidence limit is $p_{\text{lower}} = \alpha^{1/n} = (0.05)^{1/20} \approx$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_val_str` (`{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_pct_str` percent); the corresponding failure-probability upper confidence limit is `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.failure_upper_pct_str` percent.

**Systems insight**: The observation "`{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_runs_str` out of `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_runs_str` passed" supplies a confidence limit under those sampling assumptions, not an observed failure rate, a mean interval between failures, or a deployment permission. Inverting the bound gives the trials a target needs, $n = \lceil \ln\alpha / \ln p_{\text{target}} \rceil$\index{Clopper-Pearson method!sample size bound}, so a $99.9$ percent success lower limit requires `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_req_999_str` consecutive zero-failure trials drawn from the target distribution.
:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Physical failure boundaries for autonomous mobile robots and manipulators are established in @sec-body-archetype-matrix.
:::

Evaluation closes the learning loop of Part II. Evaluating the twenty clean runs that opened this chapter turns the experience logged in @sec-data and the weights trained in @sec-training into a concrete decision about the physical claim those trials can support. Each trial measures the whole machine rather than the policy alone. It records the policy's proposals, the permission path's decisions, and the Body's response, including which out-of-distribution proposals the permission path rejects, which it misses, and how much stopping margin remains.[^fn-eval-safety-enforcement]

[^fn-eval-safety-enforcement]: **Runtime safety enforcement**\index{Runtime safety enforcement}: A separately validated permission path can reject proposals that violate measured state, freshness, and actuator constraints. Its detection coverage, worst-case response time, and available stopping clearance must be tested for the implementation; a 1 kHz sampling rate alone cannot guarantee interception before contact.

The twenty-run result leaves three questions open: what outcome was sampled, what each test regime can expose, and which hazards remain outside the evidence. Finite trials bound only the distribution they sampled, so an evaluation is complete only when it also names the conditions it did not cover and the runtime monitors the permission path needs for them. A success rate means nothing until the population it was drawn from is written down.

## Metric Coverage and Limitations of Scalar Success Rates {#sec-evaluation-what-measured}

In conventional machine learning, evaluation routinely distills model capability into a single scalar summary statistic: an 85 percent Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet, an F1 score of 0.88 on a retrieval benchmark, or a token perplexity of 12.4 on a frozen language corpus. In software ML engineering, that scalar is treated as an intrinsic, reproducible property of the frozen neural weight tensor $\theta$. If two engineers evaluate $\theta$ on the same held-out validation split on separate compute clusters, they obtain identical numbers up to floating-point rounding.

This static paradigm creates the **offline evaluation illusion**: the mistaken belief that lower offline validation loss, higher action cosine similarity, or smaller Mean Squared Error (MSE) on logged data indicates superior real-world physical performance. In Physical AI, that interpretation is fundamentally invalid. A learned policy has no independent physical performance. What an evaluation bench measures is the closed-loop execution of an entire coupled cyber-physical system across a specific sequence of days, physical states, and hardware instances. Offline loss functions $\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \|a_i^* - \pi_\theta(s_i^*)\|^2$ score predictions along frozen demonstrator trajectories where errors are instantaneously erased at each clock cycle. In reality, physical success rate is an empirical property of the coupled system, comprising the policy, mechanical plant, computational hardware, operating environment, and trial protocol.

To evaluate a policy, an engineering team executes a sequence of discrete physical runs. A single trial is fully determined only when every variable that can alter the physical state trajectory is fixed or explicitly sampled. Formally, let a single trial condition be defined by a tuple $c = (s_0, e, m, \pi_\theta, \kappa)$, drawn from an operational testing distribution $\mathcal{D}$. The vector $s_0$ represents the initial state of the machine, including pose in the Special Euclidean group $\mathrm{SE}(3)$\index{SE(3) pose} (three-dimensional position and orientation), linear and angular velocities, and joint encoder positions. The environment vector $e$ captures external variables such as floor friction ($\mu$), ambient illuminance, obstacle geometry, and ambient air temperature. The machine state $m$ captures physical and hardware properties drawn from the fleet manufacturing distribution $\mathcal{M}$, encompassing unit-to-unit mechanical tolerances, battery state of charge, payload mass, tire wear, mechanical backlash\index{Mechanical backlash} in harmonic drive gearboxes, and sensor calibration matrices. The computational configuration $\pi_\theta$ encompasses the frozen policy weights $\theta$, inference quantization, scheduling deadlines, and software versions. Finally, the termination protocol $\kappa = (T_{\max}, g, \phi)$ defines the execution time limit $T_{\max}$, the spatial goal region $g$, and the binary evaluation function $\phi$ that maps the resulting trajectory to a terminal outcome $Y \in \{0, 1\}$.

In static machine learning benchmarks, inputs $(x_i, y_i)$ are sampled independently from a static data distribution $p_{\text{data}}(x, y)$. In Physical AI, the continuous trajectory $\text{Traj}(c) = (s_0, u_0, s_1, u_1, \dots, s_T)$ is generated sequentially by the closed-loop physical state transition kernel:
$$s_{t+1} \sim \mathcal{T}(s_t, u_t; m, e), \quad a_t = \pi_\theta(s_t), \quad u_t = \text{Gate}(a_t, s_t)$$
The true success probability under this evaluation protocol is the expected value of the binary task outcome averaged over the joint distribution of trial conditions:
$$p(\mathcal{D}) = \mathbb{E}_{c \sim \mathcal{D}}[\phi(\text{Traj}(c))]$$
(@sec-appendix-ml-trajectory-distribution gives the formal integral). In test engineering, the abstract distribution $\mathcal{D}$ is operationalized through a **stratified test matrix** or Latin hypercube sampling grid across controllable parameters—systematically varying payload mass, approach speed, illumination, and initial spatial standoff—while logging uncontrollable environmental parameters such as ambient temperature and floor friction. Unstratified, naive random sampling is inadequate because it oversamples benign nominal states while leaving boundary regions unvisited.

Here $\text{Traj}(c)$ is the continuous physical trajectory produced when the policy $\pi_\theta$ executes within the physical environment and hardware state defined by $c$. This dependency demonstrates why success probability cannot be treated as a measurement of $\theta$ alone. The model weights $\theta$ constitute only one parameter inside the condition vector $c$. If the distribution over floor friction changes, or if battery voltage sags along its discharge curve, the physical transition kernel $\mathcal{T}$ shifts and the expected success rate changes while $\theta$ remains identical. The sampling protocol is not an external apparatus measuring an isolated model; it is part of the mathematical quantity being estimated.

::: {#dfn-evaluation-closed-loop-estimand .callout-definition title="Closed-loop evaluation estimand"}

***Closed-loop evaluation estimand***\index{Closed-loop evaluation estimand!definition}\index{Evaluation estimand!definition} is the expected physical task outcome $p(\mathcal{D}) = \mathbb{E}_{c \sim \mathcal{D}}[\phi(\text{Traj}(c))]$ defined over the joint distribution of initial states, mechanical plant wear, environmental physics, frozen policy weights, and evaluation predicates:
$$c = (s_0, e, m, \pi_\theta, \kappa) \sim \mathcal{D}$$
rather than an intrinsic property of the neural policy weights evaluated in isolation.

1.  **Significance**: In static machine learning, held-out accuracy is treated as a property of the model $\pi_\theta$. In physical AI, substituting a worn tire, letting battery voltage sag, or shifting ambient illuminance alters the physical state transition function without changing a single weight. The sampling distribution of operational conditions $\mathcal{D}$ is an inseparable part of the quantity being estimated.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike open-loop validation metrics (such as validation loss, cosine similarity, or mean squared trajectory error) which score predictions against frozen recorded states, the closed-loop estimand integrates over the endogenous feedback loop where past actions physically move the machine, directly changing the future sensor observations it will receive.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Reporting a single success rate percentage without predeclaring the support, density, and environmental bounds of the test distribution $\mathcal{D}$. Any physical policy can be made arbitrarily successful by testing exclusively in benign, unperturbed states.

:::

### Hardware instance variance and environmental unobservables

The physical mechanisms that alter $c$ between trials operate independently of the policy, and the mobile manipulator exhibits each of them across two major sources of dispersion: **hardware instance variance** and **environmental unobservables**.

First, hardware instance variance reflects the physical reality that robotic production lines do not manufacture identical copies. Even within the same manufacturing batch, robots exhibit unit-to-unit mechanical tolerances:

- **Gearbox backlash and compliance**: Harmonic drive gearboxes in the arm exhibit machining tolerances resulting in joint backlash ($\Delta \theta_{\text{backlash}} \sim 0.5\text{ to }2.0\text{ mrad}$). Under direction reversals, this deadband introduces non-linear hysteresis and phase lag that destabilize tight neural feedback loops.
- **Structural link compliance**: Elastic link deflection under payload varies across chassis assemblies, shifting the true Tool Center Point (TCP)\index{Tool center point} relative to forward kinematics calculations.
- **Sensor assembly misalignments**: Real-world camera mounts and depth sensor brackets deviate by $\pm 1\text{ to }3\text{ mm}$ and $\pm 0.5^\circ$ from CAD nominals, introducing systematic coordinate frame offsets between sensor frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{cam}}$ and base frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{base}}$.
- **Actuator electrical variance**: Motor phase resistances and torque constants ($K_t$) vary by up to $\pm 5$ percent across stator windings. Furthermore, as the battery discharges\index{State of charge (SoC)}, the drives lose voltage headroom against back-electromotive force (back-EMF)\index{Back-EMF}, shifting the torque-speed curve\index{Torque-speed curve} and diminishing acceleration authority.

Second, environmental unobservables alter the physical interaction dynamics without changing camera pixels in a way the neural network recognizes. Ambient daylight shifting across the warehouse alters illuminance, causing camera auto-exposure to stretch shutter times, inducing motion blur during base turns. Direct solar glare at dawn or dusk saturates complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) sensor arrays, washing out visual contrast at the latch interface. On the floor, dust accumulation and ambient humidity alter the tire-floor friction coefficient ($\mu$), extending braking distance. In the manipulator arm, repeated door openings generate Joule heating ($I^2 R$)\index{Joule heating} in motor windings and warm harmonic drive lubricants, decreasing damping and expanding link dimensions. Consequently, the tool-center point meets the latch at a different spatial offset on a hot afternoon than on a cold morning. A policy evaluated across twenty trials on Unit 01 in the morning may fail completely when tested on Unit 02 in the afternoon, despite running identical frozen weights.

The reset procedure moves $c$ as well. An operator who repositions the base after a difficult run may favor an easy start, and an automated reset that repeats one path heats the windings cyclically. An operator who catches a failing run and discards it as a reset erases the hardest failure from the sample. Statistical evaluation must therefore distinguish sampling variation from a change in the estimand. When $n$ trials are drawn from a fixed $\mathcal{D}$, the sample proportion $\hat{p} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n Y_i$ fluctuates around $p(\mathcal{D})$, and standard estimators bound that noise. Loading the tote rack or moving the door's strike plate changes the experiment to a different distribution $\mathcal{D}'$ with its own $p(\mathcal{D}')$, and pooling the two samples combines observations from two different machines.

### Intervention-based physical metrics

In academic machine learning, success is conventionally reduced to a binary indicator $Y \in \{0, 1\}$. In Physical AI systems engineering, scalar success rate is an impoverished, dangerously misleading metric. A manipulation trial that successfully opens a door only because an alert human safety operator repeatedly grabbed the arm to prevent it from gouging the frame is not an autonomous success. Conversely, an autonomous run that halts safely 2 centimeters before a collision because a Control Barrier Function (CBF) vetoes an unsafe command is a success of the safety envelope, but a failure of the policy.

To characterize physical operational competence rigorously, test engineering replaces scalar success rates with a multi-dimensional suite of **intervention-based physical metrics**:

1. **Autonomous Completion Rate (ACR)**: Let $I_i \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ be the total count of supervisory interventions (whether by human operators, runtime CBF veto gates, or emergency tripwires) during trial $i$, and let $Y_i \in \{0, 1\}$ denote goal achievement within the time limit $T_{\max}$. The unassisted autonomous success indicator is defined as:
   $$A_i = \mathbb{I}(Y_i = 1 \land I_i = 0)$$
   The Autonomous Completion Rate is the sample proportion of completely unassisted trials:
   $$\text{ACR} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n A_i = \frac{N_{\text{unassisted}}}{n}$$
   ACR enforces the principle that a trial requiring even a single protective override is a failure of autonomous policy authority ($A_i = 0$), even if the physical task eventually reaches completion.

2. **Mean Time Between Interventions (MTBI)**: Where MTBF measures unmitigated plant destruction, MTBI measures the frequency of safety-envelope boundary violations during active execution:
   $$T_{\text{MTBI}} = \frac{T_{\text{active}}}{N_{\text{int}}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n t_{\text{active}, i}}{\sum_{i=1}^n I_i}$$
   where $t_{\text{active}, i}$ is the active operating duration of trial $i$ and $N_{\text{int}} = \sum_{i=1}^n I_i$ is the total number of recorded interventions. MTBI directly quantifies supervisory burden: an autonomous fleet with an MTBI of 15 minutes requires continuous operator supervision, whereas an MTBI of 500 hours enables unassisted commercial deployment.

3. **Intervention Density ($D_{\text{int}}$)**: In spatial navigation and continuous trajectory tracking, interventions must be normalized against physical exposure distance or discrete control steps:
   $$D_{\text{int}} = \frac{N_{\text{int}}}{\sum_{i=1}^n L_i} \quad [\text{interventions per kilometer}] \quad \text{or} \quad D_{\text{int}} = \frac{N_{\text{int}}}{\sum_{i=1}^n T_{\text{steps}, i}} \quad [\text{interventions per } 1{,}000 \text{ steps}]$$
   where $L_i$ is the path distance traversed. Intervention density exposes whether policy degradation is uniformly distributed or concentrated at specific geometric bottlenecks (such as narrow doorway passages).

4. **Reset Latency ($T_{\text{reset}}$)**: In physical qualification campaigns, the true experimental cost is governed by the time required to recover the plant and environment after a trial concludes or aborts:
   $$T_{\text{reset}} = t_{\text{physical\_restore}} + t_{\text{calibration}} + t_{\text{telemetry\_flush}}$$
   If a manipulation task takes 25 seconds of active execution ($t_{\text{run}} = 25\text{ s}$) but requires 60 seconds of manual reset latency ($T_{\text{reset}} = 60\text{ s}$) to clear jammed latch pins, recalibrate joint encoders, and return the base to its initial standoff, the reset latency consumes over 70 percent of test-cell occupancy. Campaigns with high reset latency create intense organizational pressure to take shortcuts—such as skipping motor thermal cooldown or repositioning the robot to easier initial poses—which corrupts trial stationarity.

::: {#dfn-evaluation-intervention-metrics .callout-definition title="Intervention-based physical metrics"}

***Intervention-based physical metrics***\index{Intervention-based physical metrics!definition}\index{Autonomous Completion Rate!definition}\index{Mean Time Between Interventions!definition}\index{Intervention Density!definition}\index{Reset Latency!definition} quantify autonomous policy performance through the frequency, spatial density, and recovery overhead of runtime safety overrides:

- **Autonomous Completion Rate (ACR)**: $\text{ACR} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{I}(Y_i = 1 \land I_i = 0) = \frac{N_{\text{unassisted}}}{n}$, requiring zero overrides for unassisted success.
- **Mean Time Between Interventions (MTBI)**: $T_{\text{MTBI}} = \frac{T_{\text{active}}}{N_{\text{int}}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n t_{\text{active}, i}}{\sum_{i=1}^n I_i}$, measuring operational supervision burden.
- **Intervention Density ($D_{\text{int}}$)**: $D_{\text{int}} = \frac{N_{\text{int}}}{\sum_{i=1}^n L_i}$ or $\frac{N_{\text{int}}}{\sum_{i=1}^n T_{\text{steps}, i}}$, normalizing interventions against exposure distance or discrete control steps.
- **Reset Latency ($T_{\text{reset}}$)**: $T_{\text{reset}} = t_{\text{physical\_restore}} + t_{\text{calibration}} + t_{\text{telemetry\_flush}}$, tracking physical cell recovery downtime.

1.  **Significance**: In static machine learning, held-out accuracy is a scalar score over frozen test samples. In physical AI, scalar success rates ($Y \in \{0, 1\}$) obscure policy inadequacy whenever runtime safety envelopes, Control Barrier Functions, or human safety operators intervene to prevent collisions. A system with zero hardware damage can still suffer an unacceptably low MTBI (such as an intervention every three minutes).
2.  **Distinction**: While Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) measures unmitigated hardware destruction outside the safety envelope, MTBI, ACR, and $D_{\text{int}}$ measure policy competence inside the safety envelope. Conflating censored interventions with unassisted survival commits the censored trial fallacy.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Omitting Reset Latency from qualification budgets. When manual resets consume 70 percent of test-cell occupancy, operators face intense organizational pressure to bypass motor thermal cooldown periods or favor easier initial conditions, breaking trial stationarity.

:::

Because success probability and intervention rates are defined only with respect to a specific joint distribution $\mathcal{D}$, the intended operating region must be declared before trials are sampled. The **target Operational Design Domain (ODD)**\index{Operational design domain!target ODD} is the part of the declared ODD (@sec-training-policy-manifest) that the evaluation samples; its sampling weights define $\mathcal{D}$, and no evaluation claim reaches beyond it. If an engineering team executes fifty physical runs across ad hoc trajectories and reports a 90 percent pass rate, the denominator corresponds to an undefined population. A measured success rate supports a target-distribution claim only when the support and sampling weights of $\mathcal{D}$ are specified in advance, establishing explicit bounds on illuminance, payload ranges, surface friction coefficients, allowable initial state offsets, and the specific hardware serial numbers tested.

Extracting valid confidence bounds from empirical trials requires three operational conditions:

1. *Independent and Identically Distributed Sampling:* Trials must be independent realizations drawn from $\mathcal{D}$. In static ML, shuffling the validation split ensures independent samples. On physical hardware, thermal accumulation in motor windings ($I^2 R$), battery voltage sag, and progressive mechanical backlash create temporal autocorrelation across trials. Run 20 is fundamentally not drawn from the same physical distribution as Run 1 unless adequate thermal cooldown and battery recharging intervals are strictly enforced. Furthermore, trials executed on a single hardware unit (Unit 01) cannot be treated as i.i.d. draws from the fleet distribution $\mathcal{M}$.
2. *Fixed Outcome Predicates:* The binary evaluation function $\phi$ and the termination criteria $\kappa$ must remain fixed throughout the campaign. Modifying the time horizon $T_{\max}$ or adjusting the spatial tolerance of the goal region $g$ midway through testing alters the definition of success, committing post-hoc metric drift.
3. *Full-Denominator Accounting:* Every initiated run that aborts due to hardware faults, communication timeouts, or safety-rated emergency stops (e.g., exceeding the collaborative-robot power and force limits of ISO 10218\index{ISO 10218} / ISO/TS 15066\index{ISO/TS 15066}) must be recorded as a failure ($Y = 0$, $A = 0$). In static ML, dropping test samples that are hard to classify is recognized as blatant data tampering. In robotics, discarding aborted runs or safety interventions as "invalid hardware glitches" is the exact physical equivalent: it substitutes a conditional measure of execution on surviving hardware for the true operational reliability of the machine. When a runtime safety monitor or human supervisor intervenes to prevent plant destruction, the trial is censored before damage occurs. What the testbed measures is an intervention event; the operational metric of competence inside the safety envelope is the Intervention Rate and Mean Time Between Interventions (MTBI), whereas MTBF measures unmitigated plant destruction. Conflating censored runs with unassisted survival is the **censored trial fallacy**. Dropping aborted or intercepted trials masks physical vulnerability.

When these conditions hold, physical trials yield an unbiased sample mean for the closed-loop system under $\mathcal{D}$. Physical trials are also slow, so evaluation workflows often substitute open-loop scoring on recorded datasets, which measures how accurately a candidate reproduces logged expert actions. That substitution assumes that accurate prediction of demonstrated actions carries over when the policy's own actions choose its next state, and only the closed loop can test it.

## Closed-Loop Dynamics {#sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics}

In standard deep learning pipelines, model performance is evaluated by computing empirical risk across a static held-out validation split $\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}} = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^N$:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \ell(f_\theta(x_i), y_i)$$
Whether the target metric is Top-1 classification accuracy, token perplexity, F1 score, or action regression loss, evaluation is fundamentally passive and decoupled. The data-generating process is feedforward and memoryless with respect to the model's predictions: mispredicting sample $i$ has zero causal influence on sample $i+1$ ($\partial x_{i+1} / \partial \hat{y}_i = 0$). Relying on this static paradigm in embodied autonomy produces the **offline evaluation illusion**: the false assumption that minimizing regression loss or maximizing action cosine similarity against static logs translates to safe, stable closed-loop execution.

In Physical AI, this decoupling vanishes entirely. Actions cross the causal boundary into mass, momentum, and non-smooth contact mechanics. The policy's admitted actions physically move the plant, endogenously creating subsequent sensory inputs ($s_{t+1} = f(s_t, u_t)$). Actions are not classifications; they are physical forces, torques, and velocity setpoints that interact with inertia, friction, and backlash. A navigation policy can reproduce recorded aisle runs almost perfectly under static regression metrics, yet spend the base's entire clearance to a storage rack before traversing a third of the aisle. The difference lies in what each kind of test feeds back to the policy.

In an **open-loop evaluation**\index{Open-loop evaluation!definition}, a candidate policy $\pi_\theta$ is scored across a static dataset of recorded demonstrations $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{demo}} = \{(s_t^*, a_t^*)\}_{t=1}^T$. At each discrete timestep $t$, the policy receives a recorded demonstrator state $s_t^*$ and outputs a predicted action $\hat{a}_t = \pi_\theta(s_t^*)$. An error metric, such as mean squared error or cross-entropy, measures the distance between $\hat{a}_t$ and the recorded expert action $a_t^*$. At step $t+1$, the evaluation pipeline supplies the next recorded state $s_{t+1}^*$ from the dataset. The action $\hat{a}_t$ produced by the policy is discarded without executing on hardware, keeping the sequence of input states independent of the policy's past outputs ($\partial s_{t+1}^* / \partial \hat{a}_t = 0$). In a **closed-loop evaluation**\index{Closed-loop evaluation!definition}, the policy proposes $a_t = \pi_\theta(s_t)$; the permission path checks it against measured state and constraints, applies $u_t$ (or a fallback), and the plant evolves as $s_{t+1} = f(s_t,u_t)$. The applied command changes the physical state and later observations, crossing the causal boundary in @sec-boundary-causal-boundary.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/spa_locator_as.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="S·P·A locator triad highlighting the Act-to-Sense feedback edge."}
*The Act $\rightarrow$ Sense feedback closure: actions physically perturb the environment, altering subsequent sensory observations.*
:::

### Compounding error and kinematic integration {#sec-evaluation-compounding-error}

Why does a neural policy that achieves negligible open-loop validation loss drive a physical robot off course within seconds? Open-loop evaluation tests actions exclusively along the demonstrator's static state trajectory, where inputs are forcibly reset to expert states at every clock cycle. In closed-loop deployment, because the policy's own admitted actions physically move the mechanical plant, small prediction errors immediately perturb subsequent sensor observations.

Formally, consider an execution horizon of $T$ steps where a candidate policy $\pi_\theta$ incurs an expected single-step error bounded by $\mathbb{E}_{s \sim d^*}[\ell(s, \pi_\theta(s))] \le \epsilon$ under the expert demonstrator distribution $d^*$. In an open-loop evaluation, because past errors are erased by dataset resets, the cumulative loss scales strictly linearly with horizon $T$:
$$\mathbb{E}_{\text{open}}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T \ell(s_t^*, \pi_\theta(s_t^*))\right] \le T \epsilon$$
In closed-loop execution, however, the state sequence is generated endogenously: $s_{t+1} = f(s_t, \pi_\theta(s_t))$. An uncorrected error at time step $t$ shifts the robot into an unmodeled state distribution $d_t^{\pi_\theta} \neq d^*$. Because the policy has never been trained on recoveries from that perturbed state, in the worst case it continues to make errors on all remaining $T - t$ time steps. Summing these unmitigated error cascades across the full horizon yields the quadratic compounding covariate shift bound [@ross2011reduction]:
$$\mathbb{E}_{\text{closed}}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T \ell(s_t, \pi_\theta(s_t))\right] - J(\pi^*) \le \sum_{t=1}^T (T - t + 1)\epsilon = \mathcal{O}(T^2 \epsilon)$$
Under continuous physical kinematics, this statistical compounding has an exact physical counterpart: an uncorrected heading or steering bias integrates forward into macroscopic lateral displacement, causing the robot to exhaust its safe clearance envelope.

```{python}
#| label: calc-evaluation-aisle-heading-drift
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HEADING BIAS AGAINST THE AISLE'S SIDE CLEARANCE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics, @fig-07-open-vs-closed-loop,
# │          and the takeaways.
# │ Show: where a persistent 1 degree heading bias of the navigation stack
# │       (not the evaluated latch policy) spends the aisle's side clearance.
# │ How: y(t) = v sin(eps) t; t_impact = W_clear / (v sin(eps)); the side
# │      clearance is (aisle width - machine width) / 2.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_time, fmt_angle, fmt_math, sci_latex, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class AisleDrift:
    """Closed-loop drift of a biased navigation policy on the running machine's aisle."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative; drive limit
    clearance = AISLE.side_clearance  # category: illustrative; side clearance each side
    aisle_width = AISLE.aisle_width  # category: illustrative; site geometry
    aisle_length = AISLE.aisle_length  # category: illustrative; site geometry
    machine_width = RM.footprint_width  # category: illustrative; base footprint
    heading_offset_deg = 1.0  # category: illustrative; persistent heading bias

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    eps = math.radians(heading_offset_deg)
    eps_q = eps * radian
    angular_mse = (eps_q**2).to(radian**2)  # open-loop score on recorded centerline states
    t_impact = (clearance / (v * math.sin(eps))).to(ureg.second)
    x_impact = (v * t_impact).to(ureg.meter)
    aisle_fraction = (x_impact / aisle_length).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second).magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9, "Drive limit is not 1.5 m/s")
    check(abs(clearance.to(ureg.meter).magnitude - 0.15) < 1e-9, "Side clearance is not 0.15 m")
    check(abs(((aisle_width - machine_width) / 2 - clearance).to(ureg.meter).magnitude) < 1e-9, "Side clearance must equal (aisle - machine) / 2")
    check(abs(aisle_length.to(ureg.meter).magnitude - 30.0) < 1e-9, "Aisle length is not 30 m")
    check(abs(x_impact.to(ureg.meter).magnitude - 8.6) < 0.05, "Clearance should be spent in about 8.6 m")
    check(abs(t_impact.to(ureg.second).magnitude - 5.73) < 0.005, "Clearance should be spent in about 5.7 s")
    check(aisle_fraction < 1 / 3, "Prose says less than a third of the aisle")
    check(abs(heading_offset_deg - 1.0) < 1e-12, "Prose, fig-cap, and fig-alt state a 1.0 degree heading offset")
    check(abs(angular_mse.magnitude - 3.05e-4) < 5e-7, "fig-alt states an angular MSE of 3.05e-4 rad^2")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, precision=1)
    clearance_str = fmt_length(clearance, precision=2)
    aisle_width_str = fmt_length(aisle_width, unit=ureg.centimeter, precision=0)
    aisle_length_str = fmt_length(aisle_length, precision=0)
    machine_width_str = fmt_length(machine_width, unit=ureg.centimeter, precision=0)
    clearance_cm_str = fmt_length(clearance, unit=ureg.centimeter, precision=0)
    t_impact_str = fmt_time(t_impact, unit=ureg.second, precision=1)
    x_impact_str = fmt_length(x_impact, precision=1)
    eps_rad_str = fmt_angle(eps_q, precision=5)
    angular_mse_math = fmt_math(rf"{sci_latex(angular_mse.magnitude)}\text{{ rad}}^2")
    angular_mse_eq = fmt_math(rf"\text{{MSE}}_\theta = ({fmt(eps, precision=5)})^2 \approx {sci_latex(angular_mse.magnitude)}\text{{ rad}}^2")
```

Open-loop evaluation tests actions along the demonstrator's state trajectory; a policy with low offline prediction error can fail when its biased proposals are admitted to physical motion, because its own actions carry it off the states it was trained on. This is the endogenous-data principle (\ref{pri-vol4-endogenous-drift}); @sec-data-endogenous-experience developed its consequence for data, and evaluation must measure it on the machine. The door campaign cannot show the effect, because its base stands still while the arm works, so the example comes from the same machine's navigation stack rather than from the latch policy under evaluation. The base drives a `{python} AisleDrift.aisle_length_str` aisle at its `{python} AisleDrift.v_str` drive limit (both illustrative), and the nominal expert demonstration follows the centerline with heading $\theta^* = 0\text{ rad}$ and lateral offset $y^* = 0\text{ m}$. Suppose the candidate navigation policy has a systematic heading bias of $\epsilon_\theta = 1.0^\circ$ (`{python} AisleDrift.eps_rad_str`) on every step, and the permission path admits each of these proposals because none is infeasible on its own while clearance remains.

In an open-loop evaluation, the policy receives the demonstrator state $s_t^* = (x_t^*, 0, 0)$ at each step and predicts a forward velocity with a $1.0^\circ$ steering offset. The offline scoring pipeline records a mean absolute angular error of $1.0^\circ$ (`{python} AisleDrift.eps_rad_str`) and an extremely low mean squared error of `{python} AisleDrift.angular_mse_eq`.[^fn-math-openloop-mse] In closed-loop execution, however, because the machine physically moves based on previously admitted commands, uncorrected heading errors compound continuously over time. Under planar unicycle kinematics ($\dot{y} = v \sin \theta \approx v \epsilon_\theta$), a persistent angular offset integrates into a cumulative lateral displacement:
$$y(t) = \int_0^t v \sin \epsilon_\theta \, d\tau \approx v \epsilon_\theta t$$
If the policy exhibits a persistent yaw-rate bias $\omega_{\text{bias}}$ (steering drift) rather than a fixed heading offset, the heading angle itself grows linearly over time ($\theta(t) = \int_0^t \omega_{\text{bias}} \, d\tau = \omega_{\text{bias}} t$). Integrating forward velocity $v$ then produces a cumulative lateral excursion that compounds quadratically in time:
$$y(t) = \int_0^t v \sin(\omega_{\text{bias}} \tau) \, d\tau \approx \frac{1}{2} v \omega_{\text{bias}} t^2$$
This continuous double integration provides the exact kinematic realization of the discrete $\mathcal{O}(T^2 \epsilon)$ compounding covariate shift bound.

For the constant $1.0^\circ$ heading bias, the base is `{python} AisleDrift.machine_width_str` wide in a `{python} AisleDrift.aisle_width_str` aisle, which leaves $W_{\text{clear}} =$ `{python} AisleDrift.clearance_cm_str` of side clearance to the rack on each side, and the drift spends that clearance at
$$t_{\text{impact}} = \frac{W_{\text{clear}}}{v \sin \epsilon_\theta},$$
which at the drive limit is `{python} AisleDrift.t_impact_str`, after `{python} AisleDrift.x_impact_str` of travel and less than a third of the way down the aisle (@fig-07-open-vs-closed-loop).[^fn-math-closedloop-lateral] Either the permission path's clearance check stops the base short of the rack or, without that check, the base strikes it. Both outcomes are a failed trial that open-loop scoring rated near-perfect.

[^fn-math-openloop-mse]: **Metric scale masking in regression loss**\index{Evaluation!metric masking}: Aggregating squared steering errors across thousands of validation frames obscures severe, intermittent directional mistakes. A single localized prediction spike of $15^\circ$ is mathematically washed out when averaged across hours of straight aisle driving. A brief angular spike can matter if its integrated motion exhausts clearance before the independent permission path responds; the outcome requires a plant and timing model.

[^fn-math-closedloop-lateral]: **Kinematic integration of heading bias**\index{Kinematics!lateral trajectory drift}: Holding heading at a constant $1.0^\circ$ offset produces linear lateral drift $y(t) = v \sin(\epsilon_\theta) t$. When steering rate is biased, unmitigated yaw integration yields quadratic drift $y(t) \approx \tfrac{1}{2} v \omega t^2$, accelerating impact with side racking.

::: {#psp-evaluation-open-loop-blindness .callout-perspective title="The offline evaluation illusion"}
Offline validation loss, Mean Squared Error (MSE), and action cosine similarity score predictions along frozen demonstrator trajectories where errors are erased at every clock cycle. Closed-loop dynamics decide physical survival: small prediction biases compound quadratically ($\mathcal{O}(T^2 \epsilon)$) into boundary excursions, and non-Lipschitz contact discontinuities ($F = k \Delta x$) turn sub-millimeter errors into destructive shock loads. Evaluating tensor mimicry offline is blind to the causal feedback loop of physical autonomy.
:::

The aisle example shows both reasons that an open-loop score\index{Open-loop evaluation!closed-loop gap} decouples from closed-loop survival. First, static evaluation cannot integrate a persistent error into displacement. It resets the machine to an expert state at every clock cycle, masking the compounding of integration errors, whereas in closed loop the state at index $t$ is the expanded composition of all previous actions:
$$s_t = f(f(\dots f(s_0, u_0)\dots, u_{t-2}), u_{t-1})$$
A persistent heading bias needs no software bug, since differential tire wear, camera-mast vibration, or floor camber produces one. Second, static evaluation cannot follow the machine into the unfamiliar states that early errors steer it toward. The first admitted error moves the base from the demonstrated state $s_1^*$ to an unvisited state $s_1$, and once it drifts a few centimeters off the centerline it occupies states absent from $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{demo}}$. The offline metric, computed only where $y = 0\text{ m}$, holds no evidence about $\pi_\theta(s)$ for $y \neq 0\text{ m}$, and a policy never shown recoveries from off-center states can make larger errors there, accelerating the divergence that @sec-training-synthesis-regimes traced for behavioral cloning.

### Contact discontinuities and metric masking {#sec-evaluation-non-lipschitz-contact}

The disconnect between offline metrics and physical survival deepens when the machine transitions from free-space kinematics to physical contact. At contact interfaces, mechanical dynamics cease to be Lipschitz continuous, and standard statistical averages fail to capture mechanical risk. Rigid-body contact involves velocity jumps ($v^+ \ne v^-$), impact shock, and set-valued Coulomb friction cones ($F_{\text{friction}} \in [-\mu F_n, \mu F_n]$). In this regime, standard offline evaluation metrics suffer from severe structural blind spots:

1. **Why action cosine similarity fails**: In representation learning and behavior modeling, action cosine similarity:
   $$\text{Cosine}(\hat{a}, a^*) = \frac{\hat{a}^\top a^*}{\|\hat{a}\| \|a^*\|}$$
   is widely used to measure directional alignment between predicted and expert commands. In physical contact, however, cosine similarity is dangerously deceptive because it completely discards command magnitude. Directional alignment without force calibration is useless: a policy proposal with 0.999 cosine similarity that commands 25 percent insufficient force stalls against the latch spring without overcoming static stiction ($F_t < \mu_s F_n$), stranding the robot indefinitely. Conversely, a proposal with 0.999 cosine similarity that commands 150 percent of the required force drives the gripper into rigid structural yield, tripping the `{python} EvalMachine.f_trip_str` contact tripwire and shearing the latch mechanism.

2. **Why action mean squared error fails**: In offline supervised validation, Mean Squared Error:
   $$\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{d} \sum_{j=1}^d (\hat{a}_j - a_j^*)^2$$
   weights every millimeter of position residual equally, regardless of physical context. In open-space transit, an end-effector tracking deviation of $2\text{ mm}$ is benign and easily recovered. But at a rigid steel latch boundary where local environmental stiffness reaches $k_{\text{contact}} \approx 5 \times 10^5\text{ N/m}$, an unmitigated $2\text{ mm}$ commanded penetration into the surface attempts to generate a normal reaction force:
   $$\Delta F = k_{\text{contact}} \Delta x = (5 \times 10^5\,\text{N/m})(0.002\,\text{m}) = 1{,}000\,\text{N}$$
   This instantaneous load exceeds the structural yield rating of the harmonic drives by an order of magnitude. Offline MSE treats this catastrophic boundary violation identically to an innocuous $2\text{ mm}$ drift in free space.

3. **Hardware instance variance at contact boundaries**: The sensitivity of contact dynamics exacerbates **hardware instance variance**. Unit-to-unit variations in joint backlash ($\Delta \theta_{\text{backlash}} \sim 0.5\text{ to }2.0\text{ mrad}$) and camera mounting tolerances ($\pm 1\text{ to }3\text{ mm}$) shift the spatial boundary of the contact interface. A policy trained on demonstrations logged on Unit 01 will encounter the physical latch surface earlier or later on Unit 02. Because contact is non-smooth, this microscopic spatial shift triggers immediate contact bifurcations: the arm either stalls in free space short of the latch or impacts the frame prematurely, causing physical jamming that offline evaluation on recorded logs can never expose.[^fn-math-contact-bifurcation]

The arm shows this exact disconnect in contact. An end-effector position error of a fraction of a millimeter per step scores as negligible Cartesian error offline, but on the latch that offset acts as a wedge. The latch's stiffness turns the lateral displacement into a reaction force ($F_{xy} = k_{\text{env}} \Delta_{xy}$) that climbs past the `{python} EvalMachine.f_trip_str` contact tripwire, which ends the attempt before the door unlatches.

[^fn-math-contact-bifurcation]: **Non-Lipschitz contact bifurcation**\index{Contact mechanics!bifurcation}: Rigid-body contact is not Lipschitz continuous, because friction cones are set-valued and impacts produce velocity jumps ($v^+ \ne v^-$). A sub-millimeter deviation in gripper contact location can switch the trajectory from stable force regulation to slip or jamming, a discontinuity that open-loop scoring on recorded states cannot expose.

Offline scores can also mislead in the pessimistic direction when the task admits several valid actions. If the demonstrator passed an obstacle on the left, an open-loop score penalizes a candidate that passes on the right (the two-mode case of @sec-training-synthesis-regimes), although in closed loop both reach the goal. An action-level error measures divergence from one recording, not satisfaction of the task.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
⇄ **Contrast:** Open-loop prediction loss contrasts with the photon-to-actuation age-of-information bounds analyzed in @sec-perception-cost-ingestion.
:::

     "3.05 times 10 to the minus four"    = AisleDrift.angular_mse_math (the fig-cap and prose use it inline)
     "1.5 meters per second"              = AisleDrift.v_str (RM.base.max_velocity, the drive limit)
