These ceilings force an architectural conclusion. Physical AI safety cannot rest on statistical confidence in the learned weights, and classical control offers no analytical substitute for the proposer. This reality represents an **architectural paradigm shift**: high-assurance safety is never certified by black-box statistical testing of unverified neural policies. Because demonstrating failure rates of $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-9}$ per hour demands millions to billions of physical hours—exceeding bearing fatigue life by orders of magnitude—safety must be guaranteed by deterministic architectural decomposition: delegating hard physical invariants to low-dimensional runtime monitors and Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) below the proposal boundary, while statistical trials on the neural policy evaluate only task completion and intervention rate inside the safety envelope.

A classical controller is certified by a **Lyapunov function**\index{Lyapunov function!stability certification} $V(\mathbf{x}) > 0$ with $\dot{V}(\mathbf{x}) \le -\gamma V(\mathbf{x})$ over a stated region, not by counting runs, and with disturbances an input-to-state stability\index{Input-to-State Stability!classical control} argument bounds the state error by the size of the input under its own model assumptions. A learned proposer carries no such stability certificate. Checking the decrease condition through its non-smooth activations is a non-convex search over millions of parameters, its latent inputs carry no physical units on which to build $V$, and contact discontinuities break the smoothness the proofs assume. Outside its training distribution a learned policy can also change its output abruptly, so that a shadow or a camera glint flips the direction of a proposed motion. The burden of proof therefore moves off the proposer and onto a low-dimensional check on an isolated microcontroller. Two strategies carry that burden, one at run time and one on the bench:

1. **Runtime Containment**: Bounding the physical authority of the learned policy by delegating the collaborative-robot force limits, kinematic acceleration limits, and emergency stops to the permission path, an independent, deterministic mechanism below the proposal boundary of @sec-boundary-machine-model. The protection claim then rests on the permission path and its fallback, whose state estimates, plant and actuator models, response timing, and reserved stopping margin must be validated separately from the policy.
2. **Fault Injection on Physical Benches**: Rather than waiting for passive disturbances to strike, engineers inject them. Injected trials follow the fault-injection method of @sec-verification-deriving-fault-list; this chapter requires only that they enter the same full-denominator ledger.

::: {#chk-eval-sample-size-mtbf .callout-checkpoint title="Sample size and MTBF evidence target"}

Before moving on, check your understanding of sample size scaling and physical test limits:

- [ ] **Exposure wall**: Under a stationary Poisson failure model, why does a one-sided 95 percent upper rate limit corresponding to a $10{,}000\text{-hour}$ MTBF target require `{python} MtbfCampaign.t_continuous_str` hours of zero-failure physical exposure?
- [ ] **Mechanical fatigue exhaustion**: Can you explain why wheel revolutions cannot be compared directly with a bearing $L_{10}$ rating without drivetrain mapping and load conditions?
- [ ] **Architectural containment vs. statistical sampling**: Can you explain why high-assurance physical AI systems substitute deterministic runtime monitors for empirical black-box trial accumulation?

:::

Even under rigorous qualification protocols and automated test cells, statistical sampling alone cannot establish ultra-reliable autonomy. What remains outside any finite campaign, and which runtime monitors the record must name for it, decides how far the evidence can carry the release decision.

## Epistemic Boundaries and Inherent Verification Ceilings {#sec-evaluation-limits}

The limits of evaluation follow from the endogenous loop of @sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics. The states a physical campaign visits depend on the commands the permission path admitted, so no fixed dataset matches the candidate's closed-loop state distribution, and a simulator substitutes its own transition model for the plant's (formal trajectory distributions in @sec-appendix-ml-trajectory-distribution). A simulator that models the aisle floor with the friction of clean, inspected concrete cannot show what the base does on a clear oil film, and one whose actuators respond instantly cannot show the lag of a real stator's electrical time constant\index{Actuator!stator delay}; the physical trajectory departs from the simulated one, and the departures compound into states no simulated run visited. A physical test therefore bounds only the distribution it actually sampled.

The strongest conclusion an empirical evaluation can support is therefore narrow, conditional, and tied to a single machine instance. The door campaign establishes that one software build on one specific hardware unit (Unit 01), from the sampled initial conditions and inside the environmental lighting and temperature present during the runs, failed with probability below `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.failure_upper_pct_str` percent at 95 percent confidence. It says nothing about a colder morning that derates the joints\index{Hardware!thermal derating}, a gearbox whose compliance\index{Hardware!gearbox compliance} and backlash have grown with wear, or a displaced strike plate.

Crucially, empirical testing on Unit 01 provides zero mathematical assurance for Unit 02 due to **hardware instance variance**:

- Unit-to-unit mechanical tolerances in harmonic drive gear teeth introduce variable backlash ($\Delta \theta_{\text{backlash}} \sim 0.5\text{ to }2.0\text{ mrad}$) that alters phase margins across physical chassis.
- Manufacturing assembly tolerances introduce subtle camera bracket angle errors ($\pm 0.5^\circ$), rotating the optical frame relative to the kinematic base and distorting 3D spatial reconstruction.
- Stator winding resistance tolerances ($\pm 5$ percent) and battery discharge curves shift actuator torque saturation limits.
- Environmental unobservables—such as diurnal solar glare angling through warehouse clerestory windows, changing floor friction from humidity, or airborne dust settling on optical lenses—shift the physical state transition kernel $\mathcal{T}$ without changing a single neural weight.

More runs on the nominal plate on Unit 01 reduce sampling uncertainty and tighten the binomial bound (@tbl-07-confidence-bounds), but they cannot reduce structural uncertainty about unmodeled physics, environmental unobservables, or hardware instance variance across the fleet. Two thousand further runs would measure that single unit with finer precision while leaving the displaced-plate cells, the loaded machine, fleet-wide unit differences, and bus jitter\index{Hardware!bus jitter} exactly as unsupported as before.

Since evaluation cannot establish how the policy behaves outside the sampled distribution, each monitorable boundary of the claim needs a runtime signal, threshold, and tested response, and the permission path must enforce independent physical constraints. Distribution support is only partially observable and an OOD detector has measurable false negatives, so conditions that cannot be sensed reliably require ODD restrictions, passive protection, or other independent barriers. The evaluation record carries these specifications in its `runtime_monitor_specs` field (@sec-evaluation-logs). The field names five monitoring channels whose coverage and response must be measured:

1. **Input Support / Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Monitor:**\index{Runtime monitoring!OOD detection} Estimates whether incoming observations depart from the tested distribution using a calibrated score and reports false negatives on held-out shifted conditions.
2. **Execution Latency Monitor:**\index{Runtime monitoring!execution latency} Measures each inference age against the declared control deadline (for example, the latch policy's `{python} EvalMachine.chunk_period_str` chunk period at `{python} EvalMachine.chunk_rate_str`), records misses, and checks that lease expiry invokes the validated fallback. A $P_{99}$ summary alone is not a hard deadline bound.
3. **Constraint Margin Monitor:**\index{Runtime monitoring!constraint margin} Tracks the distance between the current physical state and hardware safety limits, including joint torque limits\index{Actuator!torque limit}, motor winding temperature\index{Actuator!Joule heating}, and obstacle clearance against limits specified for the hardware and stopping model.
4. **Intervention Rate Monitor:**\index{Runtime monitoring!intervention rate} Calculates the frequency of permission-path overrides, detecting when policy instability causes excessive corrections.
5. **Environmental Assumption Monitor:**\index{Runtime monitoring!environmental assumptions} Measures external operating conditions, such as surface traction estimated from wheel slip and ambient illumination measured by photometric sensors.

A monitor that only writes an anomaly to a log protects nothing. When a monitor reports that a condition has left the target ODD, or that an inference missed its deadline, the permission path discards the proposal and acts on the actuators through a validated fallback, a speed restriction or a controlled stop, provided the sensed state, actuator capability, and reserved clearance make that response feasible (fallback logic in @sec-appendix-control-cbf). A timely, confident proposal still passes the independent state, clearance, and actuator checks before any $u_t$ is applied.

Some failures no software runtime monitor detects. This limitation constitutes the **epistemic trap of software OOD monitors**: an out-of-distribution detector operates entirely on digital sensor streams and latent representations. However, an optical illusion or sensor physics failure—such as a spotless clear glass partition, specular laser glare, or lens mud—causes the vision transformer backbone [@brohan2023rt1] to produce high-confidence, in-distribution latent feature tokens for an out-of-distribution physical obstacle. The software cannot detect what physical transduction failed to capture. A proposal can meet every deadline, respect every torque limit, and arise from apparently familiar latent features, yet steer the base directly into the glass partition; the measured clearance remains nominal until contact. Safety against such failures cannot come from statistical evaluation or software monitors alone. It requires physical zoning\index{Safety!physical zoning}, mechanical current limiters\index{Actuator!current limiters}, and independent physical safety barriers whose protective capability is validated independently of the learned model under specified physical assumptions.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Physical failures undetectable by sensory telemetry are formally cataloged in @sec-frontier-failures-without-detectors.
:::

These limits bind even a flawless campaign. The evidence that survives them is only as good as the campaign that produced it, and procedural and statistical errors can corrupt a campaign long before its result reaches the record.

## Empirical Evaluation Pitfalls and Metric Masking {#sec-evaluation-failure-modes}

Systematic errors undermining policy evaluation rarely stem from deliberate fraud. They arise when an evaluation protocol answers an easier question than the claim asks, creating statistical or procedural mirages that mask physical vulnerability.

### Six procedural evaluation pathologies {#sec-evaluation-procedural-pathologies}

Six recurring procedural flaws distort empirical evaluation: environment selection, metric drift, test-set contamination, optional stopping, denominator filtering, and substituting demonstrations for measurements.

**Pathology 1: Environment selection.** Environment selection occurs whenever the test bench is narrower than the claim. The twenty door runs all met the nominal strike plate at the `{python} EvalMachine.v_approach_str` guarded approach with the base stopped and the tote rack empty. If the report states their success rate as the machine's ability to open the site's cage doors, the claim silently expands to the `{python} EvalMachine.n_absences_str` unsampled cells of the ledger and the loaded machine (@sec-evaluation-limits). Environment selection\index{Environment selection} is detected by comparing a condition ledger, which records the measured strike-plate position, approach speed, payload, and floor condition of every trial, against the boundaries of the claimed domain; a ledger that covers one cell establishes nothing about the others.

**Pathology 2: Metric drift and offline surrogate substitution.** Metric drift\index{Metric drift} occurs when the evaluation metric slides from physical closed-loop task completion toward an offline surrogate such as action agreement\index{Action agreement}, validation loss, action Mean Squared Error (MSE), or action cosine similarity against recorded expert buffers. Driven by the seductive low cost of offline compute, engineering teams substitute static metrics for live rollouts. However, as demonstrated in @sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics, offline surrogates produce severe ranking inversions: cosine similarity ignores command magnitude (causing static friction stalls or structural over-torque), while MSE averages across time steps and washes out non-Lipschitz contact choke points. Metric drift is prevented by mandating that the primary evaluation metrics remain closed-loop physical observables: Autonomous Completion Rate (ACR), Mean Time Between Interventions (MTBI), and Intervention Density ($D_{\text{int}}$), with zero unmitigated tripwire crossings.

**Pathology 3: Unit-specific test set contamination.** Even with closed-loop physical trials, repeated tuning against a fixed evaluation setup degrades result independence and creates **unit-specific test set contamination**\index{Test set contamination}. When an engineering team adjusts the policy's hyper-parameters, observation filtering, or neural checkpoint after each batch of runs on a single physical testbed (e.g., Robot Unit 01 and a specific cage door), that setup ceases to be an independent holdout. Each iterative adjustment absorbs implicit information about that specific machine's individual harmonic drive gear backlash ($\Delta \theta_{\text{backlash}}$), link deflection under load, sensor bracket mounting offsets, and room lighting. After twenty tuning cycles, the resulting checkpoint achieves high success on Unit 01 because it has implicitly memorized that individual machine's mechanical quirks, but it fails completely when transferred to Unit 02 where machining tolerances differ. This unit-level contamination cannot be detected by inspecting model weights or re-evaluating on the same unit. It is detected only through cryptographic provenance tracking, auditing the chronological history of policy versions, tuning commits, and physical chassis serial numbers to confirm that final qualification was executed on fresh, quarantined machines and unvisited environmental conditions.

**Pathology 4: Optional stopping and multi-look inflation.** Evaluation protocols are equally vulnerable to unintended cherry-picking through optional stopping. When an engineer monitors a continuous sequence of physical runs and halts the experiment as soon as a target performance threshold or statistical significance criterion is reached, the reported confidence is distorted. If an evaluation team conducts an experiment where each look carries a nominal false-positive threshold of 5 percent, stopping early upon observing an apparent success across multiple evaluation checkpoints inflates the true error rate. `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_looks_str` independent 5 percent looks would have a `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_any_false_positive_pct_str` percent chance of at least one false positive. Repeated looks at one accumulating run are dependent, so the inflation for a real stopping rule must be computed for that rule. Optional stopping\index{Optional stopping} cannot be detected from summary tables or final pass rates. It is detected only by auditing the pre-registered trial protocol, verifying that sample sizes, stopping conditions, and evaluation milestones were fixed before the first physical run began.

### Sequential probability ratio testing {#sec-evaluation-sequential-sprt}

The high cost of physical rollouts creates severe pressure to stop testing as soon as a candidate policy appears viable. However, naive early stopping—peeking at accumulating outcomes and terminating when empirical success crosses a threshold—severely inflates Type I error (certifying an unsafe policy as safe). In standard machine learning benchmarks, an engineer can run a fixed validation split of $10^4$ examples without worrying about sample-size optimization because GPU inference consumes negligible marginal cost and zero physical wear. On an embodied physical machine, every trial consumes battery charge, heats motor windings through Joule heating ($I^2 R$), wears mechanical bearings, and risks mechanical shock. In fixed-sample qualification, an evaluation protocol fixes $N$ upfront (for example, $N_{\text{fixed}} \approx 65$ trials) and executes all $N$ physical rollouts to completion. If a candidate policy is defective, continuing fixed-sample testing forces the machine to endure repeated collisions, emergency stops, and chassis stress long after the evidence has decisively demonstrated failure. Conversely, if a candidate is exceptionally reliable, fixed-sample testing cannot credit that margin to terminate early without introducing the uncalibrated optional-stopping bias of @sec-evaluation-procedural-pathologies.

To terminate physical testing as early as the evidence justifies while rigorously preserving statistical error guarantees, evaluation teams employ Abraham Wald's **sequential probability ratio test (SPRT)**\index{Sequential probability ratio test}[^fn-math-wald-sprt] [@wald1945sequential]. Rather than fixing sample size in advance, SPRT evaluates likelihood-ratio martingales dynamically after each physical rollout.

Consider two predeclared operational hypotheses defined on the true operational success probability $p$:
$$\begin{aligned}
H_0 &: p = p_0 \quad \text{(unacceptable policy reliability, e.g., } p_0 = 0.90\text{)} \\
H_1 &: p = p_1 \quad \text{(acceptable target reliability, e.g., } p_1 = 0.99\text{)}
\end{aligned}$$
After observing $m$ independent physical rollouts with binary outcomes $Y_1, Y_2, \dots, Y_m$ (where $Y_i = 1$ denotes task success and $Y_i = 0$ denotes task failure, timeout, or permission-path intervention), the cumulative likelihood ratio is:
$$L_m = \prod_{i=1}^m \frac{P(Y_i \mid H_1)}{P(Y_i \mid H_0)}$$
Under the null hypothesis $H_0$, the sequence $(L_m)_{m \ge 1}$ forms a non-negative martingale with respect to the filtration $\mathcal{F}_m = \sigma(Y_1, \dots, Y_m)$ representing the observed history of physical outcomes. Specifically, evaluating the conditional expectation:
$$\mathbb{E}[L_{m+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_m] = L_m \cdot \mathbb{E}_{Y_{m+1} \sim P_0}\left[\frac{P(Y_{m+1} \mid H_1)}{P(Y_{m+1} \mid H_0)} \;\Bigg|\; \mathcal{F}_m\right] = L_m \sum_{y \in \{0, 1\}} \frac{P(y \mid H_1)}{P(y \mid H_0)} P(y \mid H_0) = L_m \sum_{y \in \{0, 1\}} P(y \mid H_1) = L_m$$
Because $\mathbb{E}[L_m \mid H_0] = L_0 = 1$ for all $m$, Doob's Optional Stopping Theorem guarantees that for any stopping time $N$ that is almost surely finite, $\mathbb{E}[L_N \mid H_0] = 1$. Crucially, Jean Ville's maximal inequality for non-negative supermartingales bounds the probability of ever exceeding an upper threshold under continuous inspection:
$$P\left(\sup_{m \ge 1} L_m \ge \frac{1}{\alpha} \;\Bigg|\; H_0\right) \le \alpha \cdot \mathbb{E}[L_0] = \alpha$$
This maximal inequality provides a profound mathematical guarantee for test engineering: **no matter when, how often, or for how long an engineer monitors accumulating physical rollouts, the probability of ever falsely accepting $H_1$ under the null hypothesis is strictly bounded by $\alpha$.** Continuous sequential monitoring under SPRT does not inflate Type I error.

Taking the natural logarithm transforms the multiplicative martingale into a cumulative additive log-likelihood ratio $S_m = \ln L_m = \sum_{i=1}^m Z_i$, where each rollout increment is $Z_i = \ln \frac{P(Y_i \mid H_1)}{P(Y_i \mid H_0)}$. For Bernoulli trial outcomes with $k = \sum_{i=1}^m Y_i$ successes across $m$ rollouts, the cumulative score evaluates in closed form:
$$S_m = k \ln \left(\frac{p_1}{p_0}\right) + (m - k) \ln \left(\frac{1 - p_1}{1 - p_0}\right)$$
Each successful physical trial increments $S_m$ by a positive step $\Delta S_{\text{succ}} = \ln(p_1 / p_0) > 0$, while each failure or safety intervention decrements $S_m$ by a negative step $\Delta S_{\text{fail}} = \ln((1 - p_1) / (1 - p_0)) < 0$. When discriminating between acceptable reliability $H_1: p_1 = 0.99$ and unacceptable reliability $H_0: p_0 = 0.90$:
$$\Delta S_{\text{succ}} = \ln\left(\frac{0.99}{0.90}\right) \approx +0.09531, \quad \Delta S_{\text{fail}} = \ln\left(\frac{0.01}{0.10}\right) = \ln(0.10) \approx -2.30259$$
Comparing the magnitudes reveals the steep **24-fold evidentiary penalty** of physical failure:
$$\frac{|\Delta S_{\text{fail}}|}{\Delta S_{\text{succ}}} = \frac{2.30259}{0.09531} \approx 24.16$$
A single mechanical jam, contact tripwire crossing, or permission-path intervention completely wipes out the accumulated evidentiary credit of more than twenty-four consecutive successful trials. In physical robotics, success is slow to demonstrate, but failure is immediately and overwhelmingly informative.

To ensure that the probability of Type I error (accepting an unacceptable policy) is bounded by $\alpha$ and the probability of Type II error (rejecting an acceptable policy) is bounded by $\beta$, testing proceeds within two absorbing decision boundaries, $B < S_m < A$, where Wald's boundary approximations are:
$$A \approx \ln \left(\frac{1 - \beta}{\alpha}\right), \quad B \approx \ln \left(\frac{\beta}{1 - \alpha}\right)$$
For standard engineering confidence parameters $\alpha = 0.05$ and $\beta = 0.10$, the decision boundaries are $A \approx \ln(0.90 / 0.05) \approx 2.890$ and $B \approx \ln(0.10 / 0.95) \approx -2.251$. At each physical rollout $m$:

1. If $S_m \ge A$: Halt testing and accept $H_1$ (policy qualified for deployment within the target ODD).
2. If $S_m \le B$: Halt testing and reject $H_1$ (policy rejected; abort campaign immediately to prevent hardware damage).
3. If $B < S_m < A$: Continue sampling; execute rollout $m+1$.

The expected physical test duration before reaching a definitive release or rejection decision is governed by **Wald's Fundamental Identity** (Wald's equation for sequential stopping):
$$\mathbb{E}[S_N] = \mathbb{E}[N] \cdot \mathbb{E}[Z]$$
Under hypothesis $H_1$, the expected single-rollout increment is the Kullback-Leibler divergence from $P_0$ to $P_1$:
$$\mathbb{E}[Z \mid H_1] = p_1 \ln\left(\frac{p_1}{p_0}\right) + (1 - p_1) \ln\left(\frac{1 - p_1}{1 - p_0}\right) = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_1 \parallel P_0) > 0$$
Under hypothesis $H_0$, the expected drift is negative: $\mathbb{E}[Z \mid H_0] = -D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_0 \parallel P_1) < 0$. Neglecting boundary overshoot, the expected terminal score under $H_1$ is $\mathbb{E}[S_N \mid H_1] \approx (1 - \beta) A + \beta B$. Substituting into Wald's identity yields the **Average Sample Number (ASN)**:
$$\mathbb{E}[N \mid H_1] \approx \frac{(1 - \beta) \ln\left(\frac{1 - \beta}{\alpha}\right) + \beta \ln\left(\frac{\beta}{1 - \alpha}\right)}{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_1 \parallel P_0)}$$
Similarly, when evaluating a defective policy under $H_0$, the expected sample size before rejection is:
$$\mathbb{E}[N \mid H_0] \approx \frac{\alpha \ln\left(\frac{1 - \beta}{\alpha}\right) + (1 - \alpha) \ln\left(\frac{\beta}{1 - \alpha}\right)}{-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_0 \parallel P_1)}$$
This derivation reveals a foundational principle for physical AI test engineering: **The expected sample size required to certify or reject a policy scales inversely with the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the target and rejection reliability distributions.**

For $p_1 = 0.99$ and $p_0 = 0.90$, the relative entropy is $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_1 \parallel P_0) \approx 0.0713\,\text{nats/trial}$ and $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_0 \parallel P_1) \approx 0.1444\,\text{nats/trial}$. Substituting these values yields an expected sample size of $\mathbb{E}[N \mid H_1] \approx 33.3$ rollouts under $H_1$, and merely $\mathbb{E}[N \mid H_0] \approx 13.8$ rollouts under $H_0$. Compared to an equivalent fixed-sample test requiring $N_{\text{fixed}} \approx 65$ trials regardless of outcomes, SPRT cuts expected physical test cycles, motor thermal rise, and bearing fatigue by 49 to 79 percent. Most importantly, when a candidate policy is defective, SPRT aborts testing after an average of only fourteen trials—sparing the testbed fifty-one subsequent collisions and preserving hardware life for viable candidates. For further details on boundary overshoot corrections and continuous-time Poisson SPRT, see @sec-appendix-ml-sprt.

[^fn-math-wald-sprt]: **Sequential Probability Ratio Test (SPRT)**\index{SPRT!sequential testing}: Predeclared likelihood-ratio boundaries allow valid sequential stopping for specified hypotheses without inflating Type I error. The expected sample size reduction follows from Wald's identity, while exact error calibrations account for boundary overshoot.

**Pathology 5: Denominator filtering and the censored trial fallacy.** A related statistical distortion occurs when the denominator of an evaluation is quietly filtered, breaking the full-denominator condition of @sec-evaluation-what-measured. A team that discards runs ending on software timeouts, emergency stops, sensor communication drops, or permission-path overrides as invalid test artifacts reports success over the surviving trials only. This denominator truncation systematically masks low Autonomous Completion Rates ($\text{ACR} = N_{\text{unassisted}} / n$) and artificially inflates apparent MTBI ($T_{\text{MTBI}} = T_{\text{active}} / N_{\text{int}}$). By discarding interrupted rollouts, nonzero intervention counts ($I_i \ge 1$) vanish from both the numerator and denominator, driving measured Intervention Density ($D_{\text{int}}$) toward zero. Furthermore, filtering omits the hidden operational overhead of Reset Latency ($T_{\text{reset}}$)—the minutes spent untangling jammed end-effectors, clearing fault registers, and physically restoring the scene—creating a false impression of rapid, autonomous operation. If the arm opens the door on nine of ten attempts and the tenth needs an operator takeover to stop the gripper wedging against the latch, removing that attempt falsely raises the apparent success rate from 90 percent to 100 percent and reports an infinite MTBI for that batch. Crucially, infrastructure aborts—such as Wi-Fi packet drops, operating system kernel thread stalls, or bus brownouts—must remain in the denominator. The physical world does not care which software or hardware subsystem failed; an autonomous forklift that stalls in an aisle intersection because of an operating system thread lock has failed its operational mission. Removing infrastructure aborts evaluates an idealized mathematical abstraction rather than the deployed cyber-physical system. When physical constraints or safety limits truncate a run before its time limit $T_{\max}$ expires, the trial is recorded as a censored failure ($A_i = 0, I_i \ge 1$) rather than omitted from the ledger. Reading survival on truncated trajectories as operational competence is the **censored trial fallacy**\index{Censored trial fallacy!definition}. Denominator filtering\index{Denominator filtering} is detected by cross-referencing low-level actuator telemetry and permission-path logs against the trial ledger, confirming that every power-on cycle, autonomy engagement, and physical reset corresponds to a recorded outcome.

::: {#ws-evaluation-nhtsa-40-percent-mirage .callout-war-story title="The 2017 NHTSA Autopilot crash rate mirage"}
**Context**: In January 2017, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) closed Preliminary Evaluation PE 16-007, which it had opened after a fatal Florida crash of a Model S operating in Autopilot mode (@sec-perception-failure-modes) [@nhtsa2017pe16007]. The closing report compared airbag-deployment crash rates in the subject Tesla vehicles before and after Autosteer was installed and stated that "the Tesla vehicles crash rate dropped by almost 40 percent after Autosteer installation," from 1.3 to 0.8 crashes per million miles.

**Mechanism**: The rate divided airbag deployments by miles driven before and after installation, and the report's own footnote noted that the rates "are for all miles travelled before and after Autopilot installation and are not limited to actual Autopilot use." The denominator therefore never measured exposure to Autosteer itself, and it was incomplete as well. A replication by Quality Control Systems Corporation found that the odometer reading at installation appears to have been reported for fewer than half of the vehicles, and that exact exposure before and after installation could be computed for only 13 percent of them [@qcs2019nhtsa]. The mileage NHTSA left uncounted, because it could be assigned to neither period, was concentrated among the vehicles with the least exposure before installation.

**Impact**: In the one cohort with complete exposure in both periods, the airbag-deployment crash rate rose 59 percent after installation, from 0.76 to 1.21 per million miles, a result the replication qualified with "if these data are to be believed." Its authors concluded that the overall 40 percent reduction was "an artifact of the Agency's treatment of mileage information that is actually missing in the underlying dataset." The replication does not measure Autosteer's effect either. It shows that the published denominator could not support the reported reduction.

**Response**: The correction came from outside the agency and two years after the closing report, because the per-vehicle mileage records that exposed the denominator were released only after a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the Department of Transportation [@qcs2019nhtsa].

**Systems lesson**: In physical AI evaluation, an unverified denominator produces a statistical mirage. Aggregating open-world mileage without engagement telemetry, operational design domain boundaries, and complete exposure records turns missing data into a safety claim. An evaluation audits the integrity of its denominator with the same rigor it applies to the failure events in its numerator.
:::

**Pathology 6: Substituting visual demonstrations for statistical measurements.** The temptation to substitute visual plausibility for statistical sampling represents a pervasive vulnerability in physical systems engineering. A single video recording of a robotic arm grasping an irregular workpiece or a mobile robot navigating a cluttered room is a demonstration, not a measurement. A visually convincing demonstration proves that the system state trajectory intersects the success set for at least one sequence of initial conditions and environmental disturbances, but it provides no information about the volume of that success set. Because human perception is tuned to smooth motion and coordinated $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ kinematics (rigid-body motions in three dimensions)\index{SE(3) kinematics}, an observer easily mistakes kinematic fluidity for policy competence. An execution that appears deliberate and smooth can operate within $10\text{ mm}$ of a kinematic singularity or carry an unmeasured $P_{95}$ tracking error that produces a collision in nine out of ten repeats. A representative demonstration has no statistical standing. A representative campaign needs predeclared sampling from the target ODD or separate per-stratum analysis, full-denominator accounting, and a sample size tied to its stated claim.

The same discipline governs comparisons. As Jacob Cohen formalized in his statistical power analysis[^fn-math-cohen-power] [@cohen1988power], deciding whether `latch-bc-01` opens the cage door more reliably than another checkpoint requires the Type I error ($\alpha$), the Type II error ($\beta$), and the effect size, the smallest difference in success rate worth detecting. Twenty runs per checkpoint carry no stated power until those quantities and the baseline success rate are known, so the protocol fixes $\alpha$, $\beta$, and the effect size before the first run.

[^fn-math-cohen-power]: **Statistical Power in Physical Trials**\index{Statistical power!sample size}: The probability $1 - \beta$ of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis. For a two-policy comparison, compute power from the baseline rate, effect size, sample allocation, and chosen test before collecting physical trials [@cohen1988power].

Each of these pathologies widens the claim beyond the evidence while leaving the report looking cleaner: a benign bench, a surrogate metric, a contaminated test door, a well-timed stop, a filtered denominator, or a persuasive video. Understanding the mechanisms by which evaluation fails clarifies the purpose of physical testing. An empirical trial is not a demonstration to convince an observer that a model works. It is an instrument to measure where policy authority fails, what physical conditions trigger the failure, and how much statistical confidence the evidence supports. Documenting those boundaries requires an immutable record that binds every trial, condition, and intervention to a verifiable physical quantity, and @sec-evaluation-logs specifies that record.

## Evaluation Logs {#sec-evaluation-logs}

When the twenty door runs are over, the record they leave behind is the only form in which the rest of the machine will ever see them, so what that record keeps decides which claims survive. Crucially, an **evaluation record**\index{Evaluation record!definition} is not a static archival compliance report; it is an active, machine-readable cyber-physical configuration manifest. As the sixth formal contract in the machine stack's 14-record lineage (serving as the Evaluation Summary contract), it formalizes the transition from Part II's statistical policy synthesis to Part III's deterministic runtime enforcement. In Part III and Part IV (runtime verification and release), the deployment gatekeeper parses the cryptographically signed evaluation record, verifies that the target ODD matches the operating site, and automatically configures runtime monitor thresholds, lease timeouts, and Control Barrier Function (CBF) parameters directly from the `runtime_monitor_specs` field at boot time. The record consumes the policy manifest of @sec-training-policy-manifest, citing it by digest, and incorporates the known absence log from the provenance record of @sec-data-policy-coverage; it adds the fields required to audit the learned policy that the manifest describes, makes no claim beyond the target ODD, and names a runtime monitor for every monitorable boundary. The record links measured outcomes to declared conditions and preserves human observations separately with their source. It serves as a self-contained evidence record that states what was measured, under what physical conditions, with what confidence, and which operational claims the resulting evidence explicitly does not support.[^fn-std-ul-sotif]

[^fn-std-ul-sotif]: **Safety of the intended functionality (SOTIF)**\index{ISO 21448!SOTIF}\index{ANSI/UL 4600!evaluation records}: ISO 21448 and ANSI/UL 4600 provide frameworks for arguing about intended-functionality and autonomous-system hazards. This chapter's immutable record is a proposed engineering evidence artifact, not a specific form mandated by either standard.

\Needspace{28\baselineskip}

| Record Schema Field           | Physical / Statistical Modality                                                                                                                                                                                          | Cryptographic & Provenance Guarantee                                                    | Downstream Verifier & Usage                                                                                    |
|:------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **`target_odd_boundary`**     | Target Operational Design Domain (ODD): the sampled cells of the declared ODD, here the nominal strike plate at the `{python} EvalMachine.v_approach_str` guarded approach under the door's own latch load, base stopped | Signed ODD specification; must lie inside the policy manifest's `declared_odd_boundary` | Defining tested conditions and calibrated OOD alerts; physical gating remains independent                      |
| **`component_hashes`**        | Policy manifest digest, frozen neural network weights ($H(\theta)$), inference engine binary, chassis serial number, unit hardware tolerances (joint backlash $\Delta \theta_{\text{backlash}}$, structural link compliance), tire batch, sensor calibration matrices, and firmware build | SHA-256 binary digests, hardware UUID, ISO 9001 calibration certificate references      | Supporting configuration traceability; preventing unrecorded hardware substitutions or unit-specific overfitting |
| **`sampling_protocol`**       | Target-distribution draw weights or per-stratum quotas, PRNG seed, reset procedure, and independence audit                                                                                                               | Automated test harness configuration script hash, telemetry sequence log                | Auditing against optional stopping and testing against hidden autocorrelation across trials                    |
| **`complete_outcome_ledger`** | Full-denominator raw outcome counts ($n_{\text{attempted}}$, $n_{\text{unassisted}}$, $N_{\text{int}}$, $n_{\text{estop}}$, $n_{\text{timeout}}$) and physical metrics ($\text{ACR}$, MTBI, $D_{\text{int}}$, and $T_{\text{reset}}$ time-series) | Monotonic microsecond hardware timestamps, uninterrupted ring-buffer telemetry          | Preventing censored trial fallacy; calculating uncorrupted empirical reliability and supervisory burden         |
| **`statistical_evidence`**    | Exact non-asymptotic Clopper-Pearson binomial lower bound, Rule of Three limit, or SPRT likelihood-ratio martingale log ($L_m$, stopping state, Type I $\alpha$ bound via Ville's inequality); Poisson rate for modeled physical exposure | Cryptographic verification signature, reproducible Python evaluation script             | Passing bounded evidence and explicit assumptions to @sec-verification                                         |
| **`unsupported_gap_catalog`** | Explicit catalog of unvisited state spaces and omitted dynamics (surface water, dynamic crowds); contains the provenance record's known absences and the manifest's omission log                                         | Declared non-support manifest, signed safety engineering sign-off                       | Parameterizing the permission path's checks, CBF constraints, and fallback policies in Part III                |
| **`runtime_monitor_specs`**   | For each monitorable boundary of the claim: signal, threshold, and tested response, across the five channels of @sec-evaluation-limits                                                                                   | Measured detection coverage and false-negative rate per channel                         | Implemented by the permission path and the observation contract's health field; read by the enforcement record |

: **Physical policy predeployment evaluation record schema**: Fields the evaluation record adds to the policy manifest it consumes, recording the target ODD, configuration digests, the sampling protocol, the complete-denominator trial ledger, non-asymptotic confidence bounds, the unsupported coverage gaps, and the runtime monitor specifications. {#tbl-07-evaluation-record-schema tbl-colwidths="[20,18,22,40]"}

The evaluation record begins with the operational claim and its formal predicates, as specified in the predeployment evaluation record schema (@tbl-07-evaluation-record-schema). It defines the mathematical success criterion, such as unlatching the cage door and swinging it open without crossing the `{python} EvalMachine.f_trip_str` contact tripwire and without a permission-path override of the policy. It bounds the target Operational Design Domain (ODD)\index{Operational design domain!target ODD}, which lies inside the declared ODD of the policy manifest, across the physical parameters that manifest names, including strike-plate position, approach speed, and the load the door presents. Finally, it names the target population of physical environments to which the result is intended to generalize, distinguishing the one cage door tested from cage doors with other strike plates or spring rates. Defining these boundaries in the record before trials begin prevents post-hoc adjustments to the pass criteria when anomalous behaviors appear.

The record captures immutable cryptographic identifiers for every software and hardware component to enable independent replication of the physical execution. These identifiers include the content hashes of the neural network weights, sensor preprocessing pipelines, policy configuration files, simulation engine builds when synthetic runs are incorporated, and the evaluation execution scripts. On the physical system, the record logs the machine chassis serial number, unit-specific mechanical tolerances—such as measured harmonic drive gear backlash ($\Delta \theta_{\text{backlash}}$) and structural link deflection under rated payload—wheel tire compound batch, sensor calibration matrices, motor controller firmware revisions, and communication bus configurations. Swapping a camera lens, altering a driver firmware version, replacing worn drive belts, or transferring the policy to a physical chassis with different mechanical tolerances alters the transfer function of the plant, invalidating the historical data if the change is unrecorded.

The record preserves the trial protocol, which was fixed before the first run so that the campaign cannot be halted at a favorable moment (the optional-stopping hazard of @sec-evaluation-failure-modes). The protocol predeclares the sample size $N_{\text{req}}$ from the claim's target and confidence, the outcome classes, and the stopping rule: a zero-failure campaign stops at its first failure and reports the exact lower bound its successes support, or completes $N_{\text{req}}$ runs and reports $\alpha^{1/N_{\text{req}}}$. A pooled binomial bound needs each condition drawn independently from the target distribution, whereas a fixed quota grid needs separate per-stratum inference and declared weights before any claim spans the target ODD. The record documents how the runs were drawn from the cells of the target ODD, the pseudorandom seed sequence governing where the base stops in front of the door, and the reset sequence executed between consecutive runs, which re-latches the door and returns the base to its `{python} EvalMachine.standoff_str` standoff. When the base returns to that standoff under autonomous control, battery thermal rise and odometry drift introduce statistical dependence between adjacent attempts. The record specifies whether trials were statistically independent or chained in series, and it registers every manual reset, hardware abort, or deviation from the pre-specified protocol.

Aggregate percentages obscure the physical failure modes that determine system risk. Each attempted run lands in exactly one predeclared class: unassisted success ($A_i = 1, I_i = 0$), reaching the goal within $T_{\max}$ with no override; censored failure ($A_i = 0, I_i \ge 1$), when the permission path overrode the policy\index{Permission path!overrides}; timeout; or hardware failure, such as a dropped bus or a faulted drive. The record reports the raw count in every class, alongside the derived physical metrics: the Autonomous Completion Rate ($\text{ACR} = N_{\text{unassisted}}/n$), Mean Time Between Interventions ($T_{\text{MTBI}} = T_{\text{active}}/N_{\text{int}}$), Intervention Density ($D_{\text{int}}$), and the cumulative Reset Latency ($T_{\text{reset}}$) incurred restoring the plant. It also reports kinematic boundary violations\index{Kinematic boundary violations} and manual emergency stops as subcounts of the class in which each affected run ended. In addition to summary tallies, the record preserves per-trial time-series metadata, including peak motor winding temperatures, maximum trajectory tracking errors, and task completion durations. Logging this telemetry ensures that nominal successes operating near thermal limits or within $5\text{ mm}$ of a hard boundary are visible during audit. Every trial initiated under policy authority remains in the denominator.

The statistical specification defines the point estimator, confidence method, nominal confidence level, sampling distribution, and underlying mathematical assumptions. For fixed-sample campaigns, it records the exact non-asymptotic Clopper-Pearson lower bound ($p_{\text{lower}} = \alpha^{1/n}$) and the continuous-time Poisson Rule of Three exposure ($T \ge 3.0/\lambda$), rejecting degenerate normal approximations. For sequential testing campaigns, it logs the operational hypotheses ($p_0, p_1$), significance levels ($\alpha, \beta$), the full likelihood-ratio martingale sequence $(L_m)_{m \ge 1}$, and the terminal stopping state ($S_N \ge A$ or $S_N \le B$), proving under Ville's maximal inequality that sequential monitoring bounded Type I false-positive risk. Alongside the supported claim, the record documents unsupported claims and known coverage gaps; the catalog begins from the known absences of the demonstration data and the omission log of the policy manifest, and adds what the trials themselves left unvisited. For each gap that can be sensed, the runtime monitor specifications name the signal, threshold, and tested response of @sec-evaluation-limits; a gap that cannot be sensed stays in the catalog as a restriction on operation.

Consider the twenty-run door campaign that opened this chapter. The latch policy opened the cage door twenty times from the `{python} EvalMachine.standoff_str` standoff at the `{python} EvalMachine.v_approach_str` guarded approach, with the base stopped and no permission-path override. An auditor reads the record's statistical evidence as the exact bound of @sec-evaluation-closed-loop-survival, a 95 percent lower confidence limit of `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_pct_str` percent, never as the degenerate interval $[1.0, 1.0]$.

The completed record exposes the structural limits of the claim, and it shows how far the evidence narrowed on its way through Part II. The scenario ledger of @sec-data-policy-coverage crossed `{python} EvalMachine.n_plate_positions_str` strike-plate positions with `{python} EvalMachine.n_speeds_str` approach speeds, `{python} EvalMachine.n_cells_str` cells in all, and the retained demonstrations supported `{python} EvalMachine.n_supported_str`, the nominal plate at the guarded approach. The policy manifest made that cell the declared ODD of `latch-bc-01`, the target ODD took in the whole cell, the twenty clean runs were drawn from it, and they bound the failure probability there at `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.failure_upper_pct_str` percent, the one-sided upper confidence limit under the tested iid distribution (@tbl-07-confidence-bounds). Everything that narrowing left out enters the coverage gap catalog as a gap the campaign inherited rather than closed. The `{python} EvalMachine.n_absences_str` cells that held zero demonstrations hold zero trials as well, and the catalog inherits the manifest's omission log, whose `{python} EvalMachine.n_omissions_str` unclosed simulator omissions, the soft penalty contact and the missing transport lag, bar this record from being reused for any checkpoint refined in simulation. The trials add a gap of their own, because the base carried nothing in its `{python} EvalMachine.rack_capacity_str` tote rack, so the record says nothing about the loaded machine. The record shows why twenty successful runs cannot support a high-reliability claim (which requires at least $n=299$ zero-failure runs for 99 percent reliability at 95 percent confidence), and it gives a fixed basis for refusing any assertion that the policy is ready for unmonitored deployment.

An evaluation record does not certify that an autonomous machine is safe. It establishes the empirical boundaries and statistical uncertainty of a single learned component operating under controlled conditions. In @sec-verification, the verification argument ingests these evaluation records as formal evidence nodes, combining policy bounds with evidence for the physical guardrails and the permission path's latencies to evaluate whether the integrated machine satisfies its operational safety case.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Non-asymptotic Clopper-Pearson trial bounds supply the empirical evidence nodes for safety cases in @sec-release-safety-cases-claims.
:::

::: {#capstone-evaluation-humanoid-crucible .callout-perspective title="Evaluating a machine that falls"}
**Question**: What does a coverage record say when every failure in an unsupported cell is a fall that damages the test article?

The mobile manipulator's failed latch trial ends at the contact tripwire with an intact arm, so its campaign can keep sampling a hard cell; a humanoid's failed trial can end the campaign's hardware.

* **Fall count is its own estimand.** A humanoid's failed trial can end on the floor with the robot under test damaged, so the record reports falls with their own denominator and confidence limit beside task success rather than folding them into one success rate.
* **The denominator is stratified before collection.** The disturbance strata (slippery floor, a change in floor compliance, a curb, a shove) and their weights are fixed in the sampling protocol before the first trial, because a campaign on a flat floor bounds nothing about the strata it skipped.
* **A demonstrator's balance does not transfer.** A human operator keeps balance with a human body, not the robot's, so a cell such as a balanced heavy reach has no valid demonstrations; it enters the coverage gap catalog as a known absence, and the campaign cannot close it with trials it cannot afford to fail.
:::

A log that fixes its denominator, strata, and coverage gaps before collection makes the record auditable, but it cannot stop a reader of that record from drawing conclusions it does not support. Practitioners still misread benchmark metrics and carry evidence beyond the target ODD in a few recurring ways, and those misreadings are the last hazard to the claim.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-evaluation-fallacies-pitfalls}

An evaluation supports claims only within its tested conditions and limits. These mistakes arise when teams extend a result beyond those limits or attribute an architectural safeguard to the learned policy.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Repeated success in a single nominal condition proves broad operational readiness.*

The door campaign repeats one condition twenty times: the nominal strike plate, the guarded approach, the base stopped, the rack empty. Under the binomial model\index{Evaluation!Binomial Model}, those runs give the `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_pct_str` percent lower bound of \ref{nbk-evaluation-derivation-20-run-lower-bound} for that condition\index{Evaluation!Confidence Intervals}, and nothing for the other cells of the ledger or a loaded tote rack that moves the arm's torque margins. Repeating the condition sharpens the nominal estimate while the deployment-critical envelopes\index{Safety!Operational Envelope} stay untested. A readiness claim must name its target ODD, allocate trials across the physical variations inside it, and report uncertainty within each tested cell. **Nominal repetition sharpens precision on a single cell; it provides zero evidence for the rest of the operational design domain.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Explicitly partition the declared ODD into a condition matrix, allocate test quotas across all operational strata, and report confidence intervals per cell rather than pooling unstratified runs.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Zero failures in 1,000 trials proves compliance with a 99.9 percent reliability specification.*

Suppose the latch policy opens the door `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_fallacy_str` times without a trip against a requirement of 99.9 percent success at 95 percent confidence. The observed success fraction is perfect ($\hat{p} = 1.00$), and textbook Central Limit Theorem Wald intervals collapse into the degenerate point $[1.0, 1.0]$ because estimated variance $\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n$ vanishes identically. Yet exact non-asymptotic Clopper-Pearson inversion ($p_{\text{lower}} = 0.05^{1/n}$) demonstrates that the true one-sided lower confidence bound is only `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_fallacy_str`, falling short of the 99.9 percent requirement (@tbl-07-confidence-bounds); certifying it requires `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_req_999_str` clean runs. A parallel fallacy occurs in early-stage pilot evaluation: observing zero failures in 20 trials ($p_{\text{lower}} = 86.1$ percent) cannot certify even a 90 percent reliability target ($n = 29$ clean runs required), let alone an industrial 99 percent reliability target ($n = 299$ clean runs required). The gap is an evidence deficit, not an empirical proof of compliance. The trial budget follows strictly from the claim and confidence level, fixed in advance, and the report must state the exact Clopper-Pearson lower bound rather than the perfect empirical fraction. **Zero failures with an insufficient sample size represents an evidence deficit, not an empirical proof of compliance.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Reject asymptotic Wald intervals at parameter boundaries; precalculate the required sample size via the non-asymptotic Clopper-Pearson bound ($n = \lceil \ln\alpha / \ln p_{\text{target}} \rceil$) or the Poisson Rule of Three ($T \ge 3.0/\lambda$), and report exact one-sided lower confidence bounds.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *High offline action agreement on static logs guarantees closed-loop physical stability.*

An evaluation report that cites close agreement with expert actions\index{Evaluation!Action Agreement} on recorded runs—such as negligible action MSE, high discrete token accuracy, low validation perplexity, or high action cosine similarity—has measured dataset imitation on frozen buffers and nothing more. The aisle policy of @sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics matched its recordings almost exactly and still spent its side clearance due to compounding covariate shift\index{Evaluation!Covariate Shift} ($\mathcal{O}(T^2 \epsilon)$). Furthermore, at non-Lipschitz mechanical contact interfaces, sub-millimeter errors that barely register in MSE trigger destructive reaction forces ($F = k \Delta x$) and mechanical jamming, producing severe ranking inversions where low-MSE policies fail while higher-MSE policies succeed. Similarly, action cosine similarity discards command magnitude entirely; a policy predicting an action in the correct direction but with 20 percent insufficient torque stalls against stiction, while 20 percent excess torque triggers joint tripwires. Offline surrogates can screen candidate checkpoints before physical trials, but a claim of closed-loop stability\index{Control!Closed-Loop Stability} rests solely on closed-loop physical observables: Autonomous Completion Rate (ACR), Mean Time Between Interventions (MTBI), and Intervention Density ($D_{\text{int}}$) counted against the full denominator. **Offline validation loss, MSE, and cosine similarity measure dataset mimicry; closed-loop physical dynamics decide survival.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Treat offline loss, action MSE, and cosine similarity strictly as preliminary screening filters; require closed-loop physical rollouts with full-denominator accounting as the sole empirical evidence for policy stability.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Peeking at accumulating rollouts and terminating testing early inflates false safety certification.*

An engineering team testing an expensive robot watches physical rollouts accumulate. After 30 consecutive clean runs, feeling pressured by hardware wear and schedule deadlines, the team halts testing and claims compliance at 95 percent confidence. This optional stopping is a major statistical trap: repeatedly inspecting accumulating data with a nominal 5 percent significance test across multiple checkpoints inflates the true Type I error rate to 20 percent or higher. Conversely, fixed-sample testing forces all $N$ trials to run even when early failures prove a candidate is dangerous. To stop early without corrupting false-positive guarantees, teams must use Abraham Wald's Sequential Probability Ratio Test (SPRT). Under SPRT, the cumulative likelihood ratio forms a martingale whose maximum is bounded uniformly in time by Ville's maximal inequality ($P(\sup_{m \ge 1} L_m \ge 1/\alpha \mid H_0) \le \alpha$), cutting average sample sizes by 49 to 79 percent while preserving exact Type I error bounds. **Ad-hoc early stopping inflates Type I false alarms; sequential qualification requires likelihood-ratio martingales bounded by Ville's inequality.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Pre-register sequential decision boundaries ($A \approx \ln((1-\beta)/\alpha)$, $B \approx \ln(\beta/(1-\alpha))$) and update the likelihood-ratio martingale after each rollout, halting testing only when cumulative log-likelihood crosses an absorbing threshold.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Crediting the learned policy with surviving transport stalls that the enforcement architecture handled.*

The mobile manipulator completes 50 nominal aisle runs, and the team credits its learned policy with tolerance to SerDes bus jitter\index{Hardware!SerDes Jitter}. A qualification test then injects a mailbox stall that outlasts the chosen `{python} EvalMachine.t_lease_str` chunk lease of @sec-nervous-cadences. The lease\index{Safety!Freshness Lease} expires, and the permission path detects the stale lease and initiates a controlled dynamic stop, analogous to a Category 1 stop\index{Safety!Category 1 Stop}, from the fallback ladder of @sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder. That response comes from the enforcement architecture; nominal completion records do not establish that the neural weights detect or compensate for the stall. Fault injection\index{Evaluation!Fault Injection} must measure the permission path's detection and stopping behavior against the available stopping distance margin, and the evaluation report must attribute the protection to the hardware mechanism that supplied it. **Do not credit unverified neural weights with safety guarantees provided by the deterministic permission path.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Conduct systematic fault injection (injecting communication stalls and sensor dropouts) to independently benchmark the permission path's stopping envelope, and attribute safety mechanisms strictly to the hardware and software layers that executed them.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Zero physical collisions or hardware damage in testing proves high autonomous policy reliability.*

When an autonomous vehicle or mobile manipulator completes an extended campaign with zero collisions, teams frequently declare that the policy achieved high reliability (e.g., claiming an MTBF equal to total run time). But if human safety supervisors or runtime Control Barrier Functions intervened repeatedly to prevent impending impacts, the system achieved zero hardware damage ($N_{\text{damage}} = 0$) only because the protective safety envelope intervened to censor the failure trajectories. What the testbed actually measured was an intervention event; the true autonomous reliability is captured by Autonomous Completion Rate (ACR) and Mean Time Between Interventions (MTBI). A system with zero bent metal that requires an intervention every 15 minutes is completely unviable for unassisted commercial deployment. Discarding these censored interventions or treating them as successful runs confuses the protective competence of the safety architecture with the operational competence of the learned policy. **Zero collisions under active safety supervision proves the efficacy of the safety envelope, not the reliability of the learned policy.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Enforce full-denominator accounting; record every supervisory takeover, CBF clamping event, and tripwire crossing as an autonomy failure ($A_i = 0, I_i \ge 1$), and report Autonomous Completion Rate (ACR), MTBI, Intervention Density ($D_{\text{int}}$), and Reset Latency ($T_{\text{reset}}$) as primary deliverables.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Qualifying a policy on a single reference robot assumes zero unit-to-unit hardware variance across the fleet.*

An engineering team executes 300 failure-free runs on a single robot (Unit 01) and declares the policy qualified for fleet release. When flashed onto Unit 02, the policy repeatedly jams or chatters. Mechanical tolerances in harmonic drive gear teeth ($\Delta \theta_{\text{backlash}} \sim 0.5\text{ to }2.0\text{ mrad}$), structural link compliance under load, camera bracket mounting angles ($\pm 0.5^\circ$), and stator winding resistance tolerances ($\pm 5$ percent) alter the plant transfer function across physical chassis. Testing on a single golden unit measures that individual unit's specific mechanical quirks, not fleet-wide reliability. Furthermore, testing at a single time of day ignores environmental unobservables—such as diurnal solar glare angling through clerestory windows, changing floor friction from ambient humidity, or motor winding heating ($I^2 R$)—that shift physical dynamics without changing a single neural weight. **Evaluating a single robot chassis characterizes that specific unit's mechanical quirks; fleet release requires stratifying trials across the manufacturing distribution.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Stratify physical qualification across multiple chassis serial numbers drawn from the fleet manufacturing distribution $\mathcal{M}$, audit unit-specific backlash and kinematic offsets, and quarantine final qualification testing to fresh units that were not used during policy development.

:::

## Summary {#sec-evaluation-summary}

Closed-loop evaluation measures the coupled policy, permission path, plant, environment, and trial protocol, so a success rate describes a declared population rather than a weight file. Because the machine's own admitted actions choose the states it reaches, which is Part II's endogenous-data principle, only trials that close the loop through the permission path measure what the proposer does; open-loop scores cannot see the drift those actions produce. A zero-failure confidence limit then bounds the sampled population under its sampling assumptions, and censoring at the edge of safe operation keeps that population inside the envelope the campaign could afford to enter. More trials narrow that bound without widening the population, and the exposure wall places rare-hazard rates beyond any campaign a physical machine can run.

The door campaign shows the shape of the claim that survives. Twenty clean runs support a lower confidence limit for the nominal strike plate at the guarded approach, with the base stopped and unloaded, and nothing about the displaced-plate cells the demonstrations never covered or about the loaded machine. The coverage gap catalog records the states no trial visited, which the endogenous-data principle predicts no dataset holds, and assigns them to independent physical constraints and a feasible fallback on the permission path rather than to the proposer, because a runtime OOD detector can miss what it has never seen.

The chapter's product is the evaluation record—the Evaluation Summary contract of this book's lineage—and four of its parts travel forward:

1. *Bounded operational claim:* The target ODD\index{Operational design domain!target ODD}, inside the policy manifest's declared ODD, where performance was empirically characterized.
2. *Reproducible configuration and ledger:* Digests of weights, firmware, and calibration, with unit-specific hardware tolerances and every attempted, aborted, and overridden trial kept in the denominator to derive honest physical metrics ($\text{ACR}$, MTBI, $D_{\text{int}}$, $T_{\text{reset}}$).
3. *Coverage gap catalog:* The known absences of the data and the manifest's omission log, plus the conditions and hardware units the trials left unvisited.
4. *Runtime monitor specifications:* For each boundary that can be sensed, the signal, threshold, and tested response that the permission path must implement at runtime\index{Runtime monitoring}.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Closed-loop evaluation and reliability"}
* **A success rate belongs to a declared population**: The rate reflects the coupled policy, permission path, plant, environment, and trial protocol. Unit-to-unit hardware instance variance (such as harmonic drive gear backlash $\Delta \theta_{\text{backlash}}$) and environmental unobservables shift physical dynamics across builds, so evaluating a single chassis bounds only that individual instance.
* **Only a closed loop dispels the offline evaluation illusion**: Open-loop scoring returns the machine to a demonstrated state at every step ($\mathcal{O}(T \epsilon)$). In closed-loop execution, errors compound quadratically ($\mathcal{O}(T^2 \epsilon)$) into drift, and non-Lipschitz contact choke points ($F = k \Delta x$) cause ranking inversions where offline MSE and action cosine similarity completely decouple from real-world survival.
* **Intervention metrics quantify supervisory burden**: Relying solely on binary pass/fail masks dangerous control excursions. High-assurance physical evaluation requires four complementary metrics: Autonomous Completion Rate (ACR) treating any override as an autonomy failure, Mean Time Between Interventions (MTBI) measuring operational burden, Intervention Density ($D_{\text{int}}$) isolating spatial choke points, and Reset Latency ($T_{\text{reset}}$) tracking plant recovery cost.
* **Zero failures bound a rate without measuring it**: Central Limit Theorem Wald intervals collapse into $[1.0, 1.0]$ at zero failures ($k=n$). Exact Clopper-Pearson inversion bounds failure probability at $p_{\text{fail}} \le 1 - \alpha^{1/n} \approx 3/n$. Twenty clean runs yield a lower bound of only `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_pct_str` percent (failing to prove 99 percent reliability, which requires $n=299$ clean runs), and a 99.9 percent lower limit needs `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_req_999_str` clean runs.
* **Sequential testing cuts physical wear via martingales**: Abraham Wald's Sequential Probability Ratio Test (SPRT) tracks likelihood-ratio martingales bounded by Ville's maximal inequality ($P(\sup L_m \ge 1/\alpha \mid H_0) \le \alpha$), eliminating optional-stopping bias. The 24-fold evidentiary penalty of physical failures ($|\Delta S_{\text{fail}}| / \Delta S_{\text{succ}} \approx 24.1$) and Average Sample Number (ASN) scaling with KL divergence ($D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_1 \parallel P_0)$) allow early rejection of defective policies, saving 49 to 79 percent of physical test cycles.
* **The exposure wall moves rare hazards to architecture**: Bounding a hazard rate $\lambda$ with zero events takes $T \ge 3.0/\lambda$ of failure-free exposure, requiring millions of hours for ultra-reliability that exceed mechanical fatigue life ($L_{10}$). Protection against rare hazards therefore rests on deterministic runtime enforcement, Control Barrier Functions, and physical barriers, never on learned policy weights.
* **An evaluation record states where its evidence stops**: Its claim stays inside the target ODD, its ledger keeps every aborted and overridden run in the denominator to derive honest reliability, and its gap catalog and runtime monitor specifications tell the runtime what the permission path must cover.
:::

Evaluating Physical AI systems forces a reckoning with the fundamental limits of empirical observation. In discrete software, code coverage metrics and deterministic unit tests can exhaustively verify logical branches. In embodied autonomy, where continuous physics collides with high-dimensional sensory inputs, empirical trials only ever sample a microscopic fraction of the operational envelope. A run of twenty, two hundred, or two thousand incident-free trials does not prove that a robot is safe; it proves only that catastrophic hazards lurk further out in the heavy tails of the distribution. The true milestone of physical evaluation is therefore not achieving a flawless scoreboard, but establishing an honest accounting of uncertainty—defining an **Evaluation Summary** that bounds the target operating domain, catalogs coverage gaps, and assigns uncovered failure modes to independent runtime monitors. As Part II concludes, the engineering focus shifts from training and evaluating models to executing the live cyber-physical loops of Part III.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From evaluation records to perception"}
Part II ends with a record that confines trust in the learned proposer to its target ODD and names the runtime monitors the rest of the machine must supply. Part III builds the runtime that meets those obligations. The first of them falls on perception, because an input-support monitor or a latency monitor can act only on observations that carry their capture time, their coordinate frame, and their uncertainty. @Sec-perception follows a measurement from the sensor to a spatial claim that the permission path can date, place, and bound before it permits motion.
:::
